items.speaker: RAHUI KATENE
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business . Twenty years ago a song was released by David Grace
that has become known as the anthem of T ūhoe. It gives focus to the refrain “Rua
Kēnana, T ūhoe prophet of the Urewera”. In doing so, it encapsulates the pride of the
people in the leadership of someone who believed that T ūhoe could and should be self-
determining.
At the turn of the century, Rua established a thriving community in Maungap ōhatu,
where land was owned and farmed collectiv ely and all proceeds shared according to
need. A community bank was established and the people gathered around. In 1916
Maungapōhatu was invaded by a troop of some 70 police in what the Supreme Court
later ruled as an illegal assault. Rua was charged with sedition. His trial in the Auckland
High Court lasted 47 days and was the longest trial in New Zealand’s history until 1977.
Of the eight charges laid against him, th e jury found him guilty of only one, morally
resisting arrest, yet he was sentenced to a year’s hard labour and another 19 months’
imprisonment. At his sentenci ng, Chief Justice Frederick Chapman told Rua: “The arm
of the law was long … That is the lesson your people should learn from this trial.”
A century later, one wonders whether history is repeating itself. On Monday, 15
October 2007 more than 300 police carried out dawn raids on homes and premises
throughout Aotearoa. The focus of the raids was in response to what was allegedly
“concrete terrorist threats”. People had s upposedly attended training camps in the
Urewera ranges.
The latest twist in the trial of these defendants is that it now appears unlikely to go
ahead as scheduled on 30 May. Some are sp eculating that with the Rugby World Cup
and an election in sight, the timeliness of such a controversial trial has come under
scrutiny. But the question we in the M āori Party ask is if there is such a focus on one
law for all, as some parties in this H ouse would have it, how is it that the T ūhoe people
continue to suffer the long arm of the law with out so much as a murmur in this House?
Why has it taken between 4 and 5 years to gather evidence on what is now nothing more
than an arms charge?
Three weeks ago 150 prominent M āori social justice activists and academics came
together in support of a submission to the Solicitor-General sponsored by lawyers
Moana Jackson and Professor Jane Kelsey. In that letter Moana Jackson spelt out the
impacts of this sorry episode, stating: “T he accused, their whanau and the whole of
Tuhoe have had this hanging over them for al most four years, unable to live a normal
life. They already carry the label of ‘terrorists’ forever”. Waiariki electorate MP Te
Ururoa Flavell has spoken frequently about  the lifelong consequen ces of the original
raids on Ru ātoki and the never-ending saga of a prosecution that has been delayed for
nearly 4 years.
Of course, although there are dire and traum
atic impacts on human lives, there are
also some very real financial costs of a 12-week trial in Auckla nd. I cannot ignore the
echoes back to 1916, when T ūhoe had to bear the substantial legal costs of the trial
against Rua K ēnana as well as the indignity of being billed for the costs of the police
18 May 2011 General Debate 18787
expedition—which, remember, was illega l—amounting to over £900. To address these
huge financial burdens, Tūhoe was forced to sell land.
We are at a time in our nation’s constitutional history when we are attempting to
build bridges and learn from our past. Iwi across Aotearoa, in a substantial gift of
generosity to this nation, have settled cl aims amounting to an equivalent of 1 or 2
percent of the true worth of what they are en titled to. Our concern with the tragic case
against the defendants in the Urewera is that any progress we make in nation-building is
hindered by justice delayed. Th e lives of the peopl e charged as a result of the police’s
Operation Eight have been on hold for too l ong. Due process of law surely requires the
right to a jury trial in an expeditious time frame. The human impact has been enormous.
Further delay is unjustifiable. It is unfair. It is unacceptable.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The facts, just like
his electorate, are seldom visited by Davi d Cunliffe. He was caught out today, badly
spanked by Bill English, as he tried to make  out that there was a great hole in the tax
story that National has been laying out over the past 3 years.  Mr Cunliffe neglected to
say that National’s tax changes have been fiscally neutral, funded by a tax switch that is
quite transparently laid out in the Budget doc uments over the past 3 years. Mr Cunliffe
has been badly undermined today by his spokesman on revenue, who has scooped the
front page of the Dominion Post off him. He will be livid about that.
He is being badly, badly exposed for a lack of a plan. If one reads his column in the
New Zealand Herald today, one will see there is a lot of guff, a lot of unfunded stuff,
and no specifics. Three months ago David Cunliffe was telling the electorate that he had
fully costed spending promises. Where are t hose promises now? Nowhere to be seen. It
is a moving feast. Do members know why? The fact is that Da vid Cunliffe does not
want Labour to win the next election. That would be the worst possible thing that could
happen to that member’s career. He knows that  if Labour wins, he is finished, and his
goal to be the Prime Minister of New Zealand will never materialise.
Meanwhile, poor old Phil Goff is stumbling out of the Takanini Countdown at the
weekend, absolutely shocked at the price of lamb chops. He seemed like a man who was
trying to pretend that he goe s to the supermarket every wee k, when in actual fact it is
completely transparent that he went in there only for political purposes, so that he could
make out that he is a man of the people and that he is really in touch with how tough it
is for the average New Zealander. Once again,  Labour failed to visit the facts—that is,
that food prices went up under that Labour Gove rnment far more than they have in the
last 6 months under this National Government. Those members can run cost of living
arguments, and they can have the chief we ll poisoner, Trevor Mallard, go on about
BMWs, painting houses, and all that sort of st uff, but until they come up with a plan for
the electorate, they will have no credibility.
I can tell members that it ha s got to be better  than slogans. You know, it is all very
well having slogans like “Higher incomes; better jobs.” Who could be against that? But
there is absolutely no substance to the whole thing. What there is, though, is $5 billion
of unfunded promises that Phil Goff has been rolling out. He has promised to find $5
billion. The other main plank of those members’ economic policy is removing GST
from fruit and vegetables. That will not get the economy going ahead.
In the Budget tomorrow we will find a firm plan for getting New Zealand back into
surplus—a firm plan for reversing the dama ge that Labour did to New Zealand over 9
long years. It is a plan that actually targets Government payments to people in need, and
in terms of KiwiSaver and Working for Fa milies will make a difference for those who
really need it. I can tell members that these tax changes and this Government’s
economic plan have been very, very popular with the electorate. This Labour m ob is
getting absolutely no traction out there.
18788 General Debate 18 May 2011
Of course, Phil Goff is out there at the front  by himself. This other lot do not mind;
they are sharpening the knives for Phil. In actual fact, those members do not really want
to win. Phil Goff will be stuck out there. David Cunliffe does not want him to win.
David Parker has his head down. He knows that if Phil Goff wi ns, that is the end of his
career as well. I do not think Trevor Mallar d wants Goff to win, either. Otherwise those
members would be pressing Phil Goff to come  up with a credible plan for getting the
New Zealand economy ahead.
We know that this economy really n eeds the re-gearing that the National
Government is bringing it. It is absolutely essential, because those members blew years
and years of record surpluses,  and wasted $1 billion on buying a trainset. At the end of
it, they handed a hospital pass to the inco ming Government, and we have been left to
clear up the mess.
I think that when the New Zealand people see this Budget tomorrow, they will know
that it is a prudent path back to surplus.  They will appreciate the pressure that this
Government has been under. They know the damage that the last Labour Government
left as its legacy. Quite frankly, I think they are very, very thankful to have John Key as
Prime Minister, and I have no doubt that they will return him come November.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The final veil of John Key and
Bill English’s Budget dance will be lifted to morrow and, according to Bill English, all
will be revealed. Everything will be laid bare ; it will be there for the whole country to
see. For weeks now we have had the teasi ng, we have had the bl ame-shifting, and we
have had the National Government soften ing us up to expect a zero Budget—a zero
Budget that has been forced upon it by the gl obal financial crisis, by two earthquakes,
by floods and droughts and biosecurity, and by borrowing and borrowing.
John Key has told some New Zealanders that they will have to tighten their belts a
few more notches. They have been told that  they will have to pay off the $16 billion
deficit mountain that we now have. It is a mountain that has all been clocked up in 2½
years of a National Government. It has been clocked up after this Government was left
with a historically low level of debt by the last Labour Government and—unlike what
was indicated in the comments of the prev ious speaker, Jonathan Coleman—with books
in a good shape. They were in such a good shape that Bill English said  that the previous
Government had put away for a rainy day.
The deficit was clocked up by John Key a nd Bill English. They decided to borrow
$2.3 billion a year for tax cuts that we coul d not afford, tax cuts for those who already
had the most. A $350-a-week tax cut has gone to somebody on $393,000 a year, and a
$28-a-week tax cut has gone to somebody on $48,000 a year . When were those tax cuts
given? They were given after the global fina ncial crisis hit this country. They were
recklessly given by the Government. Having told  us that everyone had to tighten their
belts because of the global financial crisis, it ignored that advice and gave out tax cuts
that we could not afford. It gave out tax cuts we could not afford when unemployment
was growing at an alarming rate. Month after month unemp loyment figures were going
up.
We are now told by many commentators that the so-called tax switch is a failure and
has failed thousands of New Z ealanders. The Government cl ocked up a deficit because
it did not have any sort of plan to addre ss our current or future economic and social
problems. The deficit was clocked up by a G overnment that thinks short. Everything it
does is thinking short. I have to say that it is selling this country short.
Tomorrow is Judgment Day for this Government’s Budget. A few questions will be
asked by h
ard-working New Zealanders. They will ask whether this Budget will set out
a coherent long-term strategy to fundamentally change the economy of this country and
give hope back to Kiwis that they will have a future, and one that they own themselves.
18 May 2011 General Debate 18789
Will this Budget be bold? Will it really make  the tough but fair decisions that will see
all people pay their fair share but also get their fair share? Many New Zealanders must
have woken up today, looked at the front page of the Dominion Post, and asked how it
could be fair that they pay so much tax but there are people out there who pay so little.
They will ask whether this Budget will promote innovation and use research and
development to diversify our businesses and lif t our exports to ensure that we create
more wealth. Will it reduce unemployment and will it give the over 60,000 unemployed
young Kiwis a chance to get a job in this count ry, or will there be more platitudes about
how young Kiwis are our future? What future will young Kiwis get out of this Budget?
Will there be an opportunity for them to ge t skills training and apprenticeships? Will
there be an opportunity for them to get a decent income and stay here in New Zealand?
Will it encourage savings? No, I think we w ill see a Budget of lost opportunities. There
will be backwards-forwards backwards-forwards decision-making.

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I must pull up the previous speaker, Annette
King. The tax changes that this Government br ought in have been fiscally neutral. In
fact, there is one point I will agree on: that is  not quite right, because they are fiscally
positive over the forecast period. They are not fiscally neutral but fiscally positive over
the forecast period. On the tax switch, wh ich was one of the bi ggest changes in New
Zealand’s taxation system over the last 25 ye ars, I have a question to pose to Labour
members: which bits will you un-switch? Will you cut GST? Will you hike income tax?
Will you hike—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Excuse me, Mr Speaker. Will Labour hike business taxes?
I would talk about the Budget a bit longer , but today we have  had a very, very
important announcement from Labour. Today a quite strategic move by the Leader of
the Opposition, Mr Phil Goff, seems to have  been missed. Today on the front page of
the Dominion Post he totally shattered and shafted any chance whatsoever that the
Labour Party president, Andrew Little, had of winning the New Plymouth electorate
seat. The announcement of the “Taranaki turn over tax”, the tax on dairy farmers and
farming turnover, will absolutely obliterate any chance whatsoever that Mr Little had of
even making any gains in New Plymouth or in Taranaki. For that matter, any chance
whatsoever that Labour had of making gains in any provincial or rural seat has been
blown away by what was on the front page of the paper today.
I thought that the announcement might have been a mistake, and that maybe Mr Nash
had got a bit ahead of himself, as he is wont to do. But at question time today in the
House Mr Goff continued with it. I say to Mr Goff that the point is not that the data are
wrong; it is the way you interpret the data. That is very revealing of how they—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Although the member
might have a point, I think he cannot bring you into the debate. If  we criticised you in
that way, we would be in trouble.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member is alleging that the member on his feet was using the
word “you”, then he is correct; Mr Foss shoul d not do that. But I did not hear Mr Foss
use that word. I do apologise. I had already pulled him up. [ Interruption] The House
will come to order. That petty to-ing a nd fro-ing across the House will stop. The
member should be careful about using the word “you”, because it refers to the Speaker.
Debate across the House should not be in the second person.

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speake r. As a clarification, I understand
that that member, Trevor Mallard, was not in  his regular seat and he was leaving the
Chamber when he called the point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The m ember can call a point of or der from anywhere in the House.
We are not too pedantic a bout that. But the member Tr evor Mallard is now—oh, no, he
18790 General Debate 18 May 2011
is still there. Members should resist interrupting other memb ers’ speeches unless there
is good reason to interrupt them. I am not sure that the reason there was quite as strong
as that.

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: There was a brutal attack, with the “Taranaki turnover tax”, on
Taranaki, Hawke’s Bay, New Zealand provincial and rural farming families, and jobs
associated with farming. At least Mr Nash  has front-footed it. Perhaps that is how
Labour intends to fund some of its $7 billion of unfunded promises so far.
I guess the rest of Labour’s tax policies will continue. It has the turnover tax, a
capital gains tax, and perhaps a payroll tax coming, and perhaps an increase in income
tax, which it seems to be talking about more and more. OK, fair enough, Labour has
said it will take GST off veges. OK, th e GST rate is 15 percent—funnily enough, veges
have gone down by 15 percent in recent months . Mr Nash’s speech was a brutal attack
on business and on business confidence, but I congratulate him on, and thank him for,
providing certainty about Labour policy, ab out Labour’s tax intentions, and about
Labour’s ambitions for New Zealand.
It is interesting that no t too long ago the Labour Part y was calling the farming
industry a sunset industry of New Zeala nd—in the early 1990s. Today we have the
proof of the pudding. As Labour’s tax policy starts  to roll out, we s ee that it wants to
kill off farming for good. Perhaps some of the Green members might be fans of that, but
I for one value farming. I value rural New Zealand, and I value provincial New Zealand.
It is the heartbeat and the engine room  of the New Zealand economy. I cannot
understand it: I was going to give Mr Goff th e benefit of the doubt that this move was a
mistake, but his question today revealed Labour’s true intentions of a turnover tax, a
capital gains tax, an increase in income tax, and perhaps a payr oll tax. I posed the
question very early on as to which of the National-led Government’s tax switches that
we announced earlier and put into place in th e last few years would be un-switched if
Labour was ever to form a Government. But, to be fair to Mr Nash, I congratulate him
on at least giving us some clarity as to how Labour will fund its promises.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Tomorrow is Budget day.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We do not need that kind of mindless interjection when members
get to their feet.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Accurate as the description may have been—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: We do not need that kind of comment either.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Tomorrow is Budget day, and the most interesting thing
about the Government members’ speeches today has been that they are saying hardly
anything about what the Government might want to do. There is a picture of a desperate
Government where the backbench lacks confidence in its own ministry. Those members
would rather talk about us than their own plan to get New Zealanders out of the mess
they have created.
Let us deal with some real porkies up front . The first is that National has been tax-
neutral. Well, here is the table from the pr evious Budget that shows, on page 70, a $1
billion hole over the firs t 4 years because of the tax cuts . That is the net figure. The
gross figure for Budget 2009 and Budget 2010 was—wait for it—$23 billion of tax cuts.
Much of that went on the top marginal ra te going down from 39c to 33c. Some people
benefited hugely from that, and some did not. That was a rosy-glow picture, that $1
billion hole, and it was based on GDP being 3 pe rcent higher this year than last year.
That was the red line. What happened? The black line is way belo w the red line, and
that shows that the rosy glow did not come  off. The economy is stuck in a hole and the
Government does not know what to do about it. What it has not done is m ake everybody
pay a fair share. When Mr Nash got the an swer to the parliamentary questions about
18 May 2011 General Debate 18791
dairy farmers I thought there must have been a mistake. Surely the average dairy farmer
pays more than $1,500 a year in tax, when be neficiaries pay more than that. Well, no, a
multimillion-dollar business is a great way of sheltering income, is it not? It is a great
way of sheltering income. Look at th e farmer on the front page of the Dominion Post.
[Interruption] Mr Bennett is an accountant from Hamilton. He is complicit in some of
these rorts. Wait and see: the Labour Government will clea n up this mess, and we will
be fair to all New Zealanders.
The National Government has created a multib illion-dollar deficit, the worst in New
Zealand’s entire history—the debt mountain is worse than it has ever been in our
lifetime—and it has the gall to tell New Zealanders who are already struggling to draw
their belts in, while the belts of certain c onstituencies that traditionally vote National
have been let out another few notches. And that is not right. That is why we will fight
these folks right to the line, and it is w hy we will be the Government in November
2011, when we will set about getting New Zeal and back on the road to recovery. How
does one do that? There are four simple tests.  First, get New Zealanders back to work
and build a strong economy by innovating, and by exporting, w ith the help of modern
monetary policy that does not put the exchange rate through the roof. Secondly, save
more—do not cut KiwiSaver but save more so we own our own future. Do not throw it
all away and sell off assets. Any granny knows th at if we sell the fam ily silver there is
nothing to serve tea in tomorrow. National wants to sell the family silver; they have
given it away to their rich mates. That is wrong, and that is why National is like a
McDonald’s special—for a “limited time”. The “limited time” ends in November 2011,
because we are throwing them out. We are throwing them out because Kiwis have had
enough of being told one thing that is not true.
The great untruth of this Budget is that National is not breaking any promises. John

items.speaker: Key said before the last election
items.text: “We will not cut KiwiSaver.” What has National said
this week? It has said it will cut KiwiSa ver. National said: “We won’t touch Working
for Families.” What will it do tomorrow? It will change the abatement rate on Working
for Families. It will put a new one on. It will cut Working for Families. “We won’t
touch student loans.”, National said. Wait for tomorrow. It will. All of those are broken
promises, just like “We won’ t raise GST.” What is the excuse this time? “Oh, the
changes won’t take effect until after the election—you can throw us out.” Well, then
why not put it in next year’s Budget after National has campaigned on it? Why put it in
this year’s Budget, and legislate for it before  the election? Because it does not have the
moral courage of its convictions.

items.speaker: Craig Foss
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I realise it is towards the end of the
member’s speech, but one cannot question the courage of members in any way shape or
form, or allege anything like that of other members of this House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Objection was taken. I ask the member to withdraw that last
statement.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I withdraw and apologi se. I would not impugn the
integrity of—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is all the member needs to do.

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: It is clearly Mr Cunliffe’s day today to give
the vein-popping, “flirting with delusions of grandeur” speech from the other side—full
of hollow platitudes. It is always interesting watching Labour members speak, to see
whose day it is to make the leadership bid. Clearly today was Mr Cunliffe’s day, and I
have to say it is no surprise to hear that he addressed his entire speech to the gallery,
because none of his colleagues were paying a ny attention whatsoever to a word he had
to say. So I hope he got a better response from the gallery, because his colleagues all
18792 General Debate 18 May 2011
had their heads down and could not have show n any less interest in what he had to
say—pretty much like the rest of New Zealand.
Tomorrow is Budget day and I am pleased the members opposite have realised that.
It is the closest they have come to saying anything useful all week. The Budget this year
will be yet another brick in the rebuilding of this country’s economy.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Come on!

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: That is what it will be. It will be yet another step in turning round
the complete hash that the last Labour Gove rnment left the economy of this country in.
It is election year, but this Government will not use the Budget to recklessly throw
around money in a desperate grab for votes in the way the Labour Government did. We
will not do that; we are fiscally prudent. We know that a Government has to walk the
talk.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Tell us about the farmers’ tax.

items.speaker: AMY ADAMS
items.text: I tell Mr Cunliffe that anyone can say the words; this Government is
delivering. We know that a Government has to earn the money and has to support the
people who earn the money, before a Gove rnment has anything to spend. Labour
Governments are great at spen ding, but this Government gets  in behind people who are
actually earning the money. This Budget is about a couple of th ings: it is about
controlling Government spending and getting the books back in shape, and it is about
investing in infrastructure and skills. Those are the sorts of building blocks we need to
get this economy going. Most important, in my  view, it is about rebuilding my province
of Canterbury, and that will cost over $15 billio n. We know we have to play our part in
the rebuilding of Canterbury. New Zealand kn ows that the Government has to make
changes in order to pay that bill.
This Budget will do that; it will keep us on the path to rebalancing the economy. It
will get the books back in order, and get New Zealand back into surplus. Then we can
have choices, create productive, sustainabl e jobs, and provide better incomes for New
Zealanders. Anybody can talk about that stuff.  The National-led Government is the one
delivering that stuff for everyday New Zealanders, and that is why New Zealanders will
continue to back us. That is why every sing le poll shows us that the only lot of people
they want on the Treasury benches is the Na tional-led Government. There is no interest
in Labour, no interest in the Greens, no inte rest in the “Hone Heke” tax. The National-
led Government has shown time and again that this is the party of fiscal responsibility.
New Zealanders are supporting us.
In between Labour’s squabbles and factions it tries every now and then to come up
with a big bright idea. It tries to land a c ouple of blows on us. Wh at have we had this
week? There is so much to choose from, but my favourite ha s to be David Cunliffe’s
website poll. That was great. Two days before the Budget he was polling his faithful
sheep on what they thought a bout the Budget. Best of all,  by the time he pulled down
the website there was an 88 percent support ra te for the National Budget, which was so
good that more than 24 hours before Bill Englis h delivered it, the country already loved
it! It showed 88 percent support for the Budget, which is pretty much the support I think
most polls will show. But what about the front page of today’s Dominion Post, which
shows Stuart Nash finally dropping the veil and admitting his complete financial
incompetence by suggesting we should tax businesses on their turnover. That shows
brilliance! That story had to be one of the most moronic pi eces of thinking I have seen
in a long time. Labour went out and suggest ed that $500,000 turnover was the same as
the same amount of salary. Does that not tell us how few Labour members have ever
had a productive job in their lives? If  any one of them had run a business and had even a
basic grasp of how business works, they would know the difference between turnover
and profit. If I get this right, Labour’s plan is to tax us on money we do not earn. Is that
18 May 2011 General Debate 18793
right? It would tax us on money we do not earn. I have an earth-shattering piece of news
for members opposite. Maybe farmers are paying  tax on what they actually get to keep.
That would be radical.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Under Standing Order 106, it is requ ired to wait until the end of a member’s
speech before seeking a point of misr epresentation. The member has grossly
misrepresented the Opposition, who has never suggested—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Standing Order provides for a member who has been grossly
misrepresented, not for a party, to claim gr oss misrepresentation. If the member wishes
to come back into the debate, it has to be th at he has been misrepre sented. If that is the
case, I will hear from the Hon David Cunliffe.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Speaking to your ruling, Mr Sp eaker, I appreciate that it
must be a personal reference to a member. As the party’ s finance spokesperson, I do
take a personal inference from the suggestion that we, and therefore I—I am responsible
for this area of policy—have advocated a tu rnover tax. That is certainly not Labour’s
position. It was not contained in the Leader  of the Opposition’s questions today. If a
journalist writes that on the front page of the newspaper, we cannot be responsible for
journalism.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think we have had sufficient on that. I have allowed the Hon
David Cunliffe to do this. There is some question, though,  as to whether I perhaps
should have, but I have allowed it on this occasion. [ Interruption] That is not helpful
from the honourable deputy leader of the La bour Party. I will not take it any further,
because I do not want it repeated.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: I will pick up on David Cunliffe’s point of order, and
say that Phil Goff, Leader of the Opposition,  never once said that New Zealanders are
going to tax farmers on turnover. Never! What Mr Goff has said, repeatedly, is that the
tax system has to be about fa irness. Mr Goff has said that  every New Zealander has to
pay their fair share. So Labour took the figures that had been  provided by the Inland
Revenue Department and by the Minister of  Revenue and the figures said that the
average dairy farmer paid tax of $1,500. That is  what the figures said and that is what
the statistics from the Inland Revenue Depart ment said. So the question Mr Goff posed
was whether that was fair. That is the ques tion he posed. He asked whether it was fair,
when hard-working New Zealanders, hard-wor king salary and wage earners, are paying
a significant amount of tax, that dairy farmers are paying $1,500 a year, on average.
That is all he was asking. If Mr Key had a different answer, then he should have given
it. The figure may be slightly higher—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Paul Quinn
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We have just had confirmed by the
deputy leader of Labour that in fact they have been talking about the $500,000.

items.speaker: Hon Rick Barker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not think I need any further assistance. I will hear from the
member shortly. I ask the member to resume  his seat, because a point of order was
being called and heard, and I was about to deal  with it. While that  point of order is
being dealt with, we cannot have another point of order. Let me make it very clear to Mr
Quinn that was not a point of order. If the member wishes to raise a further point of
order, I will hear it.

items.speaker: Hon Rick Barker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Members are not to use
points of order to break up a m
ember’s speech. I object to that member’s point of order
on two grounds: firstly, it was not a point of order, and, secondly, it was a point of order
taken deliberately to break up that membe r’s speech. I ask you, Mr Speaker, to defend
our members’ rights to have an uninterrupted flow of speaking.

items.speaker: Amy Adams
items.text: Mr Speaker—
18794 General Debate 18 May 2011

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I will not take any further on this matter. What is difficult for
the Speaker, of course, is that when someone  calls a point of orde r, I cannot foretell
what the issue might be, but as soon as I could hear what the member was doing, I went
to sit him down, just as the honourable member  himself, as soon as he heard what was
going on, sought to stop it as well. But I do say to members that points of order must not
be used to disrupt another member’s speech for no good purpose, unless it is an issue of
order. I will not tolerate that, and if me mbers do that repeatedly, there will be a
consequence. I call Stuart Nash, and I apologise for what happened.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I acknowledge the sum of $1,506 may be
a little low. I had a look at the figures, I we nt through them, and I could not determine a
proper figure—there may be stuff held unde r other tax codes. But Mr Goff asked
whether it was fair that, according to Inland Revenue Department statistics, the average
dairy farmer pays about $1,500 in tax when a person on the average income pays about
I would also like to take umbrage at Mr Foss’ comments. Mr Foss is chair of the
Finance and Expenditure Committee, and he stood up here and said the Government’s
tax cuts had been fiscally positive. There has been $23 billion worth of tax cuts. Mr
Foss has himself heard the Governor of  the Reserve Bank at the Finance and
Expenditure Committee say there has been no economic stimulation whatsoever from
$23 billion worth of tax cuts. The tax cuts have had no positive effect on the economy.
I will tell the House about a woman in the electorate I live in, who is called Raewyn.
Food that a year ago cost her $85 now cost s her $115. She has two children who play
sport and belong to sports clubs. Her husband drives to work in a car. He earns above
the average wage, which 75 percent of New Zealanders do not. She has taken time off
work to complete her PhD. Raewyn and her family are the sort of family we want: good
and hard-working. She is bettering herself and she will become  a very productive
citizen. Raewyn admits she is not poor, but her family is finding it very, very tough. In
Napier and around this country, budget servic es are stretched, food banks are flooded,
and social services are overrun. I ask whether this country is the sort of place we want to
live in. Is this country the sort of place we want our children and grandchildren to
inherit? It is a country with a working co re who struggle hand to mouth and where the
very wealthy just get richer. Those who ear n $1 million a year last year received a tax
cut of $1,000 a week. Someone on a median wage in Napier received about $10 a week.
Is that fair?

items.speaker: Amy Adams
items.text: Crocodile tears.

items.speaker: STUART NASH
items.text: Amy Adams does not care about the people of Napier. All Amy
Adams cares about are the very wealthy, w ho got $1,000 a week in a tax cut, when the
vast majority of New Zealanders received less than $10. Is that fair? No, it is not.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Mr Speaker—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Before, I asked a member not to make inane interjections when a
member first got to their feet and I say it again, to members on the Opposition benches
this time. There is nothing wrong with interj ections, but let the member speak first and
have something to interject about.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Today we have seen the true Labour. It has envy and hates
people making money. It does not want to see this country progress; it wants just to take
people down. A Labour member comes in here with  an article in the paper and thinks it
is God’s gift to the world to get on the front page of the paper for once. Labour
members come in here and ask questions abou t it. Labour’s leader, Phil Goff, is so keen
to get the tax on farmers argument going, yet they pull away. They have pulled away
within 2 hours of question time. We heard Stuart Nash talking about how the numbers
might be a little bit low now. They are pul ling away from  the argument, because they
18 May 2011 General Debate 18795
know they have lost. Stuart Nash is trying to win a provincial seat by going out there
and saying that businesses shoul d pay tax on their income or  turnover. That is never
going to get anywhere, and Labour will never get anywhere doing that.
Let us give Labour members a history lesson and a lesson in accounting. Revenue
minus expenses equals profit. That is wh at people are taxed on. We are not taxed on
revenue or expenses; we are taxed on prof its. It does not matter what business people
are in—whether it is farming, forestry, fishing, retail, indus trial, manufacturing, or any
business—if you want to do that to farmi ng, you do that to the whole industry in New
Zealand. Tax everybody on revenue.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Do not bring the Speaker into the debate.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Labour wants to tax everybody on revenue. Let us see how
long that lasts. Labour members should go to  South Auckland and tell those businesses
that you are going to tax them on revenue, and you will see how many people are still in
work at the end of that day. That will be the true test of Labour. Labour members do not
know what they are talking about. If you want to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: What is it that the member does not understand about the word
“you”?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I know. I understand. If Labour wants to tax revenue, then it
can do so.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It had better be a good point of order. I have just dealt with the issue
about the member using the word “you”.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: It is a separate issue. I seek your advice. On a previous point of
order in respect of the same matter, you advi sed that if personal offence was taken and
if an explanation was given th at it was not our intent to ha ve a turnover tax, then that
should be accepted.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will resume his seat. The member was not given leave
to make a personal explanation. I allowed the member, under Standing Order 106, to
clarify in a point of order a matter in resp ect of his own speech. That is a debating
matter; it is not the same as a personal explanation. Other memb ers are perfectly at
liberty to refer to the matte r again, unlike with a persona l explanation. Leave has not
been granted for a personal ex planation. A point of order was allowed for the member
who claimed misrepresentation. I have allowed that. Members have heard the
explanation, and the matter is being debated further.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That is another example of Labour  retracting in th eir points of
order to say now that they wi ll not have a turnover tax. Y ou talk to your leader, who
came into this House today and—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You have just ruled. He
immediately went back to bringing you into  the debate. He has been here many, many
years. Surely to goodness he can get through a 5-minute speech without—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Let me just remind the honourable  member that she interjected
using the word “you” only a few short mi nutes ago. I did not pull her up on it.
Interjections cannot use “you” either. I do not want members to interrupt other
members’ speeches. The Speaker will deal with minor matters like that.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Labour members want to break up this speech, because they
know they are getting a lesson in accounting an d they do not like that. They do not like
the real truth.
Let us have a look at what happened in farm
ing in the last couple of years. It is in the
most difficult times. It happened when th e payout came down. They were difficult
times. There was high debt and a low payout. Many, many farmers nearly went to the
wall. Mr Cunliffe has been at a select committee where the Reserve Bank has come in
18796 General Debate 18 May 2011
and questioned the debt levels of farmers.  He really knows what is going on, if he
would only admit it. That is  the reality of th e situation. Labour members are then
comparing payouts in high years with payouts in  low years. It is very, very naughty of
Labour members and the media to do so.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: How come there’s no profit on a record payout?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Well, that is the thing; Mr Cunliffe does not understand that
revenue minus expenses equals profit. He thinks that revenue is profit. That is the
difference. That is what Labour wants to  tax; it wants to tax New Zealanders on
revenue. It wants to go to every business in  New Zealand and tax on revenue. I want to
see Labour go out and do that. Le t us see you put that in y our manifesto, Mr Cunliffe.
That is the great Minister of Finance you want to be. You will tax the country on
revenue. The Green Party members are also talking about introducing a capital gains
tax.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member seeking a point of order? It had better be a genuine
point of order.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Under Standing Order 106 the member has transgressed again
and gone to the extent of using this member’s name.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member has already had the chance under Standing Order 106
to argue that he has been misrepresente d. Unlike a personal explanation, it is not a
matter that cannot be referred to again by the House. Member s are at liberty to debate
the matter further. The member had the chance to argue that he has been
misrepresented. The House has heard that, I allowed that, but it is not like a personal
explanation where members cannot refer to it  again. I do not want to have speeches
interrupted lightly.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Mr Cunliffe will not seek a point of order and make a personal
statement, because he will not go out ther e and say he does not believe in taxing
revenue. He does not have the guts to stand up in this House and say—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Now I will interrupt the member. This is serious; the member will
wipe the grin off his face. The member cannot allege that another member lacks
courage. We had that earlier on today. In fact, I asked the Hon David Cunliffe to
withdraw and apologise. Now I ask this memb er to get to his feet to withdraw and
apologise—and I want him to do so seriously—when I have sat down. He will sit down
now, and when I have sat down he will get to his feet and do it with some sincerity.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I withdraw and apologise. The member over there had the
chance then to make a personal statement and deny that Labour will have a revenue tax,
but he did not. He sat there and just let it go. The Green Party talks about a capital gains
tax in regard to farming. Well, there is a capita l gains tax in regard to farming, and it is
that if you sell a property with in a certain period of time th e profit on the sale can be
taxed. Also, you have a yearly capital ga ins tax on farming, unlike in any other
business, where you are taxed on livestock, and that is a capital gains tax.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Does the member not understand how to use the English language
to avoid saying “you” all the time? The memb er has just said “you” three times in
succession, “If you do this, you do that.” “If th at is done” is the way to do it. The
member should use the other part of speech.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The Green Party needs to unde rstand that when there is
taxation in the farming sector there is a livestock tax, and the livestock tax is a capital
gains tax. That is something the Green Party tends to forget.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Frankly, all I have seen today from the
Government benches is an utterly embarrassi ng display. To be frank, it began when the
Prim
e Minister rose today. You would not have known that we—
18 May 2011 General Debate 18797

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have just corrected a National member. Let me now pull up a
Labour member. Every time the member says “You would not have known”, she
implies that the Speaker would not have know n. I can assure her th at the Speaker does
know. Members should debate correctly in this House. The reason why we do not use
the word “you” is that not only does it refer to the Speaker, and the Speaker must not be
brought into the debate, but also it personalises the debate. The reason for not using that
part of speech is to avoid personal attacks in this Hous e—“you did this”, or “you did
that”. I tell members that it is a longstanding tradition. I do not want  to be unfair to Mr
Bennett by allowing Miss Ardern to get away with it. Members should not do that.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Strike one versus strike 200 is the
only point I would make.
From the Prime Minister’s contribution today, we would not know that we are on the
verge of a zero Budget. The display we saw from the Government almost implied that
what we will be presented with tomorrow will somehow be a j oyous occasion. I saw an
empathy-free comedian of ashamed proportions on that side of the House today. When
did a $16 billion deficit become funny? That is the question I have for the Government.
When did 6.6 percent unemployment become a joke? The point I wish to make today is
that at no point should we assume that the Budget that will be presented to us tomorrow
is by any means a default Budge t. Choices have been made in the lead-up to the Budget
that will be presented tomorrow that have led to the situation where we are now
considering making significant cuts in areas like Working for Families, student loans,
and KiwiSaver. All of that is as a result of choices.
The Government is very likely to make the claim that the global financial crisis and
the Christchurch earthquake are somehow the sole reason why we will be seeing these
cuts tomorrow. Let us be honest; that is simply not the case.

items.speaker: Paul Quinn
items.text: Because of the mess that the Labour Government left it in.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I can tell Mr Quinn that political commentary from
Television New Zealand is one of the few areas where I have seen the acknowledgment
that the economy was stalling well before the first Christchurch earthquake. That is for
sure. We knew that. The reason is that the G overnment never had a plan, not before and
not after. There was never a plan for growth. Let us also be honest about the three areas
the Government is now targeting. Before National came into Government, it described
Working for Families as communism and student loans as a bribe. It had never been a
fan of KiwiSaver. So it is not enough for National members to stand here and tell us that
by default the Government has no choice but to  make the cuts it is making. It had a
choice to present this country  with $2.5 billion worth of ta x cuts. That was its choice,
and it made it. Now we as a country are payi ng the consequences of  that with the cuts
we will see tomorrow. Let us also be clear about the cuts to the areas it has chosen.
National members are not wringing their hands over them. These are ideological
choices that they are making under the guise of being forced to make them by the global
financial crisis and the Christchurch earthquake.
Let us also look at the impact that this lack of growth has had. I do not want us just to
assume that it means that they have had to make a few tough calls. It has had very real
consequences for the state of our economy. The Prime Minister cr ows about projected
growth in wages and employment levels. He  has not told us what proportion of that
growth is simply down to redeployment ar ound the Christchurch earthquake. There is
6.6 percent unemployment and 27 percent of our young people are now looking for
jobs, which is the highest number we have on record. There are 77,000 young people
who are not in employment, education, or training. If members on that side of the House
do not know, I can tell them th at that is an in crease of 34,000 since they took office.
They can crow as much as they like about a ll the reasons why that has occurred, but at
18798 General Debate 18 May 2011
some point the excuses need to end and there has to be a plan for growth. A tax cut,
first, was not it, and, second, made it worse.
What have we seen the Government pr esent around employment? There have been
three attempts to tackle the issue. The J ob Summit was the first. How many jobs did the
Job Summit create? Mr Cunliffe indicates a handful. There were hundreds at best.
Secondly, we had Job Ops. Half of that package was canned af ter the Government
recognised and acknowledged that all it creat ed was short-term, make-work schemes.
All we got out of that were  pumpkin patches—short-term employment. Thirdly, we had
the employment plan. The Government was go ing to invest $55 million in skills, which
it has already cut.

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a privilege to stand
and speak in the general debate. I have h eard a lot of the arguments from across the
Chamber. From the speakers we have heard today the difference between the
Opposition and this Government is clear. It is clear that the Opposition is all about
negative tactics and pointing out the things that are goi ng wrong. I have not heard one
Opposition speaker point out a vision for this country. I have not heard one Opposition
speaker talk about the issues that matter.
In the 2½ years our Government has been in office we have b een talking about the
issues that matter. We have been talking about national standards for kids. We have
been talking about raising the achievement level for our children, particularly for the tail
end of kids who leave school without being able to write and read, which is very sad.
Opposition members have not talked about the increase in the number of elective
surgeries that has happened under this Government. They have not talked about the
integrated health-care services  that are now being rolled out across this country as part
of a vision for bringing more convenient,  more timely, and more effective health
services to our communities. They have not talked about the infrastructure investment
that this Government has put forward in te rms of rolling out broadband and the type of
road infrastructure that has certainly impacted on my community of Maungakiekie,
where the barriers to trade and commerce lie in infrastructure bottlenecks.
What we have heard from the Opposition ha s been about BMWs that they purchased
all of 4 years ago. What we have heard a bout from Opposition members has been about
the painting of a house, but the previous Government spent millions of dollars on
infrastructure such as the Governor-Gener al’s residence and the Prime Minister’s
residence. We have heard vi le personal attacks made against the Prime Minister from
Opposition members—vile personal attacks made  against the Prime Minister. I believe
they are doing that because th ey are worried. They are worr ied because when the Prime
Minister and I visited Onehunga last Frida y, he was given a standing ovation when he
walked into the Onehunga Workingmen’s Club. You know that the Labour members are
worried about that. When you go to afternoon teas where—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, no—

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: —I am sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker—350 senior
citizens of all shapes, sizes, and ethnicities turn up and they suppor t the Prime Minister
and welcome him for his positive attitude to bringing about change in this country, you
know—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member cannot bring
the Speaker into this.

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: —no, no—that Opposition members are worried.
This Budget will bring about change. This Budget will be measured and it will be
responsible. It will be about making changes to some of the $5 billion a year in
spending on Working for Families and student lo ans, as well as KiwiSaver. That much
has been canvassed. But it is also about the $54.5 million that will go into improving the
18 May 2011 General Debate 18799
safety and quality of maternity services  in this country. Women go through a major
transition in their lives in giving birth to our children, and this Government is
committed to supporting them. It is abou t the $55 million that  will go towards
supporting young people into jobs; that is what it will go in to. It is about supporting
those young people, because they are our future.
The party opposite is obviously  divorced from reality. You have the Leader of the
Opposition shopping in Takanini.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, no.

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Why is the Leader of the Opposition not shopping at
Pak ’N Save in Mount Roskill? Mr Nash is committed to taxing incomes and taxing the
turnover of businesses. Mr Nash is a bri ght man, but he is sadly mistaken in his
conviction to tax those revenue s of businesses. It is sad that you have not heard about
the good things in our community.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Just before I call the next
member I just wish to advise members, for th eir benefit, that every time a member uses
the word “you” the member is referring to the Chair. The member must refer to a
Minister or another member as “the Minister ” or “that member”; that is, in the third
person. I refer members to Standing Order 103.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker Robertson. Two
nights ago, along with maybe 500 othe r concerned Wellingtonians, I attended
atmospheric physicist and National Aeronautics and Space Administ ration director Dr
James Hansen’s lecture on climate change. Dr Hansen is in New Zealand to highlight
the risk of climate change to our planet and to future generations. He says our global
climate is nearing the tipping point. Change s are beginning to appear and there is
potential for explosive changes, with effects that will be irreversible if we do not rapidly
slow the growth of fossil fuel emissions ove r the next few years.  In particular, Dr
Hansen is here to raise awareness on coal, which he describes as the single greatest
threat to civilisation and all life on our planet. Coal is the biggest threat because it is the
largest source of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and the one easiest left in the ground.
Dr Hansen’s tour coincides with an important point for our New Zealand future. The
Government is actively encouraging, thr ough its draft energy st rategy, the hugely
expensive think big plan to destroy valuable Southland farmland to dig up dirty lignite
coal, which will destroy our climate credenti als and our valuable “clean, green” brand.
Over the last 10,000 years the Earth’s climate has been remarkably stable, fluctuating
by less than 1 degree centigrade over that period. This has enab led civilisation to
develop in a safe, constant environment. Th is has led to the society we see today.
Preservation of life as we know it on this plan et requires us to stab ilise emissions at or
below 350 parts per million. We are currently  at 391 parts per million and rising by two
parts per million a year. This Government has an inadequate emissions reduction target
of 50 percent by 2050. However, even this lowl y emissions target will be impossible to
meet if the Government allows the lignite plans to proceed. This is the height of
irresponsibility, and, as Dr Hans en repeatedly points out, climate change is a scientific
issue but, more important, climate change is  a moral issue requiri ng us in New Zealand
to keep the coal in the hole.
What does all this mean for New Zealand? We market ourselves as clean and green
on the world stage. However, Dr Hansen says of New Zealand that the fact the
Government is even thinking of digging up the lignite shows there is a huge gap.
Lignite is at the coalface of the New Zeala nd environmental crisis. It is estimated that
New Zealand has around 6.2 billion tonnes of  economically recoverably lignite. The
trouble is lignite is the most  inefficient and amongst the mo st polluting types of coal
there are. Nevertheless, Solid Energy and othe rs are pushing their pr oposals to mine it,
18800 General Debate 18 May 2011
ignoring the critical report from the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment
that claims mining just is not worth it. We  are dismally failing our current climate
change target, and allowing the lignite conversion to go ahead will signal to the world
we have given up on our emissions reduction targets and our valuab le “clean, green”
brand. If the proposed lignite mining goes ahead, our emissions look set to rise
drastically—as much as 20 percent of our country’s emissions from one lignite-to-diesel
plant. Lignite trashes our “clean, green” br and and our international climate treaty
credibility.
Under this National Government’s emi ssions trading scheme, the plans could
potentially cost the taxpayer $275 million a year from carbon credit subsidies the miners
would receive. Over a lifetime, the cost of just  one lignite-to-diesel plant is likely to be
in the order of billions of dollars. It is clearly bad for the Government’s books, and bad
because it locks in polluting industries. In oral questions today th e Acting Minister of
Energy and Resources attested there would not  be subsidies. However, either she has
not read the report from the Parliamentar y Commissioner for the Environment or she
has changed the rules without telling anyone el se. Lignite coal has environmental costs,
fiscal costs, and also significant opportunity costs. The capital invested in these projects
should be going to cleantech, greentech project s that are greener, cheaper, and will last
us for ever.
Dr Hansen is in New Zealand and is talking about his grandchildren as his
motivation for tackling the climate crisis. By the time my son Arlo, who is now 3 years
old, starts school we could have an ice-free Arctic in summer. By his 10 th birthday we
will have likely increased the atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations more than in
the preceding 150,000 years of natural emissions . By the time he starts high school we
could have lost more than 3,000 cubic kilometr es of ice from Antarctica and Greenland.
I want my son, his children, and the children and grandchildren of everyone else in this
room to grow up in a world with a stable c limate. In this Chamber we will not be the
ones to bear the impact of our  irresponsible acti ons; it will be our children, and their
children, and every generation to come, not to mention every other species with which
we share this, our only planet. Kia ora.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: I start by referring to the lunacy we have just
heard from the Green Party member Gareth Hughes. Last night I sat in the Banquet Hall
along with the member from the West Coas t, Chris Auchinvole, and heard a great
presentation from a West Coast mining gr oup. It pointed out that mining on the West
Coast produces about $700 million to $800 milli on a year of export income, and with a
little bit of help and a little time it could produce another $1 billion of export income for
New Zealand. That mining produces jobs and ta xes, which produces the real wealth for
New Zealand.
This is the problem that we have with  the Opposition. Opposition members either
cannot count or do not want to understand how real wealth is created in New Zealand.
Last night in this Chamber we heard Clare Curran trying  to subtract 800,000 from 1.6
million. She got 83,000. This morning we see in the Dominion Post that a journalist, for
whatever reason, has pointed out that an  income of $500,000, which was the revenue
turnover of a business, should be the basis for taxation. At question time today we heard
the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Phil Goff, point out and reaffirm that a turnover tax in
some shape or form is the way to go. I am surprised.
I look across at members on the other side and I give them cr edit. I look at Mr
Cunliffe. He is a smart man. He has spent some time advising major corporations
around the world—so I thought. I thought that no  way would that man come up with an
idea like this. Well, it turns out that maybe we were wrong. Mr Nash came up with that
brilliant idea. It would take  $5 billion to f und the hole that exists in Labour’s
18 May 2011 General Debate 18801
expenditure programme—$5 billion. Fonterra has a $60 billion turnover. I know—let us
tax them at 10 percent. That will be the solution! That will solve everything!
When we go through the proce ss it is like that old politic al saying about cows. We
have two cows, we look after the cows, and they produce milk. The Labour Party has a
view. If the farmer has two cows, then take  a cow, produce the milk, and throw it away.
That is the Labour Party’s focus. We heard from Jacinda Ardern  that jobs in places like
Pumpkin Patch are not real jobs. I say to th e member who pointed that out that people
working in retail—the thousands of peopl e up and down the country working in shops
for 8 or 10 hours a day, like my family does—are working in real  jobs. They produce
real value for New Zealanders.
That is what Opposition members do not und erstand. People have  to create real
wealth. They have income, they deduct their ex penses, and that is ca lled profit. That is
what we tax in New Zealand. There is nothi ng imaginary. There are no pixies at the
bottom of the garden creati ng wealth that we can just throw at projects for the
Opposition’s great, grandiose plans.
We have heard, over time, some of that cr aziness from Labour members. They told
us that we would have an 11 percent unemployment rate; we have 6.5 percent. They
told us we would have 20,000 people unemploye d in Christchurch alone, but that was
absolute rubbish. They tell us that the soluti on is to borrow more money so we can save
it right now. Well, right now New Zealand has a mortgage, an overdraft, and a credit
card balance in deficit, and its creditors are banging on its door. It would be absolutely
ludicrous to go and borrow more money just to put it on a lottery that is the sharemarket
we are seeing right now.
Those Labour members, seemingly, believe  that National members have no idea.
Well, I point to last year’s Budget. We rel eased an investment plan to outline, for the
first time ever, the way we would spend mo re than $100 billion over the next 10 years.
We were the first Government in the history of New Zealand to do that. It is a plan to
invest in our infrastructure in the smartest  way possible, and it has never been done
before in the history of the New Zealand Parliament. But what credit do we get from
members on that side? They ask where the plan  is. I tell them that tomorrow they will
see a plan. They will see a plan outlined to bring the Budget into balance.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I hope so—for New Zealand.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: We cannot carry on spending more money than we earn, I tell
Mr Cunliffe. We cannot go on borrowing $300 million a week and spending the $5
billion that that member, and his party, wants to continue to spend, to bankrupt not only
me, not only my family, but this whole count ry. That is what Labour’s spending would
achieve. Thank you.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I will take a brief call on the Westpac New
Zealand Bill, to thank and acknowledge members in the Chamber, who will, no doubt,
speak to the bill, the Business Committee for helping with the process of this bill, and of
course the members of that Business Committee.  It goes without saying that I am also
thanking party leaders around the Chambe r and acknowledging their cooperation—in
and out of the Chamber, I guess—various finance spokespersons, people who were
referenced to help with this legislation, and of course members. I also acknowledge
Finance and Expenditure Committee members. I was absent during the second reading,
18802 Westpac New Zealand Bill 18 May 2011
but I looked at and reviewed some of the speeches there, and those members captured
what we did at the select committee pretty well, I think.
I will make just one quick point, because I noticed that a point was raised and a
question asked of me, as the chair of th e Finance and Expenditure Committee and the
member whose name is on the bill, about whether there were any issues with the bill. I
can assure the Committee, and the Chair, that all processes and procedures were correct,
and that members were always aware of the b ill and able to make fair representation on
it. I can assure the Committee that no issues whatsoever were raised. Nor do I think
there are any issues.
The bill is relatively straightforward. So me members in the Chamber would have
spoken on the previous bill, upon which this b ill rests, which was the bill of 2006 in the
name of the Hon Marian Hobbs. That bill turned into the Act of 2006.
There has been quite a bit of consultation about the bill. There is general and very
good understanding of what the bill is actually facilitating, and members have been very
reassured, I believe, by the assurances from the Reserve Bank, from the Inland Revenue
Department, from Treasury, and from the Ministry of Justice, under the New Zealand
Bill of Rights Act and the checks and balances that the ministry does. Those
