items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I welcome back
colleagues to the Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: We’ve been waiting all night for this.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Absolutely. It is the highlight of Mr Tremain’s evening—
and perhaps life—to be here for this.
When I was last speaking I was worki ng my way through the memorandum of
understanding between the Royal Society of New Zealand and the Council for the
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18839
Humanities, because it lies at the heart of this purpose clause. Essentially, the
memorandum of understanding is bringing toge ther the Council for the Humanities and
the Royal Society in a way in which both or ganisations will be able to work closely
together and to ensure that the kaupapa, th e philosophy and values, of the organisations
are kept. I think I had come to the point of saying that  the term “human ities” will be
included in all places within the Royal Society’s mandate and on its website. We will be
doing that as we work through the bill th at is before us. Also, in making its
representations to the Government and ag encies, the Royal Society will be including
humanities wherever it is relevant, and part icular representations will be made about
humanities. Obviously in collaboration with  the Council for the Humanities, which will
become the Humanities Committee of the Royal Society, there will be a particular focus
on promotion and celebration of the humanities.
I thought it was important to put on the record what the memorandum of
understanding between the Roya l Society and the Council for the Humanities means in
terms of this purpose clause. I think it is  a very good document that gives a solid
foundation to the way in which the two organisations will now work together and it will
allow the purpose clause to be enacted. I think this is a very important document. It
shows that the level of collaboration be tween the Council for the Humanities and the
Royal Society has been high for some tim e. They are committed to bringing this
together. In fact, they have largely incorpor ated most of the work required to bring it
together and this legislation is merely the legal requirement on top of that.
In one last point on this memorandum of understanding, as I said in the last
intervention, one aspect of the memorandum  of understanding is the statement that
within 5 years the Royal Society will use its best endeavours to have its Act reflect the
inclusion of the humanities. We are well ahead of time, because this was negotiated in
February 2010, so we have until February 2015  to pass this legislation. As I said the
other day, it might take that long.

items.speaker: Hon Pete Hodgson
items.text: It won’t take that long.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I say to Mr Hodgson that it probably will not, but we
certainly want to give it a thorough consid eration this evening as we work our way
through the clauses. At the end of this cal l I will seek the leave of the Committee to
table this memorandum of understanding because I believe that it is an important part of
the debate. I seek the leave of the Committee to table the memorandum of
understanding between the Royal Society of New Zealand and the Council for the
Humanities.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is anyone
opposed to that course of action? It appears not. Leave is granted.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hon PETE HODGSON
items.text: I think the memorandum of
understanding will be pretty useful, and I hope it will be made available to members
soon. I was going to ask three questions about the memorandum of understanding, but
one of them has been answered, and that is the date it is being written in. The second
question relates to whether the memorandum of understanding was its elf subject to any
scrutiny by the academy council or the academy executive committee. The member in
the chair, Grant Robertson, may want to refl ect on that. I would assume that there has
been consultation. I would further assume th at in the course of the memorandum of
understanding there would have been—I do not want to use the term “argy-bargy”; that
is not appropriate for the Royal Society—car efully considered variances of view as
people trolled through the vicissitudes of their various disciplin es to see whether
incorporating the humanities into the memorandum of understanding, and therefore into
18840 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011
the purpose of the Royal Society of New Z ealand Amendment Bill, was a legitimate
thing to do. The member may choose at his le isure to give us some insight into the
process by which the memorandum of understanding is drafted.
I think the more important thing for memb ers of the Committee in general is to
reflect on the words in the memorandum of und erstanding that the member referred to
when he said that where it was appropriate the Royal Society, in making representations
to Government, would consider whether the humanities had something to offer. That is
an area that I think we need to look at a little more deeply.
Later on in the bill—and I appreciate that we are talking only on clause 4—when we
get to section 6(e) in clause  7, it states that it is a function of the Royal Society “to
provide expert advice on important public  issues to the Government and the
community:”. From now on, that expert advi ce will include the advice that we can
divine from the humanities. Let us reflect on  what that might be. A good way to do that
is to go to the British humanities scholars hip group—the British humanities council, the
body of people in Britain who involve themse lves with humanities. I suppose in an
effort to sell humanities to the British public, it produced a book about the sort of
information that humanities might offer a Government of the day that might be helpful
to the Government of the day. The book came out at about the time of the London
bombings, so it inevitably incl uded a piece of research in which some sociologists and
those who wanted to study the phenomenology of religion spoke at length with the
imams of different parts of Britain—with th e geographical distribu tion of imams, but
also with imams from different parts of th e world; for example, those who had come
from Pakistan, from Afghanistan, northern Af rica, and so on. The researchers were able
to give, by way of this scholar ship, quite a lot of insight in to a nation that desperately
needed that insight. It is a good example, I think, of the humanities being of immediate
value to the Government of the day.
Another example, just to get our appe tites whetted—because I am sure other
members will be able to offer the Committ ee further examples—is from New Zealand,
not England. It is not an immediate example, it is historical, and it  is occasioned by the
sad death of Judith Binney, who, of course , through the la tter part of her life wrote
extensively on T ūhoe. I do not want to make any politics out of this, but the T ūhoe
claim is not advancing, or it at  least has got itself into trouble. Although I do not know
where the Tūhoe claim will go in the future—others will know more than me—it is my
assertion that when that claim is settled, people will look back on Judith Binney’s work
and say to themselves that had she not live d, it would have been a different settlement.
My assertion is that that is an exam ple whereby one person’ s scholarship, quite
narrowly defined but quite extensively done and most exhaustively written about, will
actively influence public policy that is in front of us in this country.
So let us think now about other examples  in the area called the humanities in which
we, the Government, including local government, those of us who are in the policy elite,
those of us who get to do the decision making, will be informed by the humanities in the
future and have been informed by humanitie s until now. I am asserting that we have
been ignoring the humanities; that we have been absorbing their lessons almost in an
indirect way, in an unconscious manner, an d that the humanities influence public policy
a great deal.
This comes from a scientist. If members want to know where I have been greatly
influenced by science, th ey should refer to the Royal Commission on Genetic
Modification. That is where I drew my public  policy from. It was not from any opening
or closing prejudice or predil ection or from a general view of the world, but from the
science alone. Why? Because I had nothing el se to go on. This was new. I needed to
know what the science said. It was a very good example of where science effected a
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18841
huge impact on public policy. But very often it does not, and the Royal Society would
much rather that it did more often than it doe s. I am making the case, as a scientist, not
only for science, but I am beginning to make  the case for the role of humanities in
public policy. This purpose clause is a good place to do it.
The member in charge of the bill ha s reminded us of the memorandum of
understanding that exists between the humanities of New Zealand and the Royal Society
of New Zealand to bring them together and spoke of the role of humanities when the
Royal Society was making representations to the Government or was involved in some
educative process. Those of us who think th at humanities are nice only, that they are
just poetry, should think again. Poetry may not directly affect pub lic policy a lot, but
history does and geography does. Just thi nk of the Geographic Board—people who go
around renaming things. Think of the role of the humanities in our trying to get the
nomenclature of our own place in order. It  takes a bit of time, and we do not do it
without expert advice. So there is anothe r example. I am sure many members will be
able to leap to their feet, when I return to my seat, to  give examples of where the
humanities have been instructive or have been, in some cases, perhaps even
inspirational in determining Government policy. We do not have to always rely on what
the health professionals say, what the physic ists say, what the educationalists say, or
what the social scientists or political scien tists say. We can reach to the humanities. We
can ask historians what they have to say about life.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: We all have feelings.

items.speaker: Hon PETE HODGSON
items.text: We all have feelings. We can ask people whose skill is
with language, who are skilled linguists, what they have to say about that. We all know
that this is the one country in the world wh ere there is a particular language, known as
te reo, which if it does not exist here, it will not exist anywhere. We are absolutely
beholden to the humanities for the maintenan ce of that, the teaching of language to our
mokopuna. There are a bunch of things to which the humanities make a contribution
that I think have probably been underrated.
I am coming to the view that I soon need to resume my seat. I have enjoyed this
contribution and I do thank members for their close consideration and careful attention
to my modest contribution. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: What I would like to do is to follow on
from Pete Hodgson’s contribution. I think he ma de a really important point that cuts to
the very heart of the purpose of the Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill,
which is the incorporation of the humanities into the Royal Society. I was reflecting on
his contribution as he was speaking.
The Prime Minister’s Chief Science Adviser,  Peter Gluckman, is looking very much
at the issue of evidence, and scientific evidence in particular, in terms of the
contribution that that can make to policy. Although we support that—and, of course, we
should be making decisions on the basis of  evidence—Peter Gluckman makes it quite
clear that we should at  least have the eviden ce presented before us , and as a result of
that evidence we should make the decision. We  may decide to take that evidence into
consideration in the decision on policy, or we may, for political reasons, decide to
ignore it or take only some of  it into consideration. But ne vertheless that evidence is
before us. Peter Gluckman makes a very good point in that regard.
However, I think what Pete Hodgson was also saying is that it is not just scientific
evidence that is important in the considera tion of policy but also history. He mentioned
te reo, the Mā ori language. That too is  important when we are looking at policy in this
particular place.
I will go back to clause 4, the purpose clause, to reflect on what the Royal Society
itself says about the inclusion of the humanities in this bill. Clause 4(a) recognis es that
18842 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011
incorporating the humanities is a big step fo rward and an important step forward for the
Royal Society to make. The explanatory note of the bill also notes that in November
2008—and Grant Robertson talked about this before, in term s of the date of this
particular legislation and how  it came into being—the council of the Royal Society
resolved that there was a need to expand th e object and the functions  of the society to
include humanities. So we are looking at this  legislation 2½ years on from when it was
first considered.
The Royal Society went on to say—and this is important—“The decision to extend
and enhance the Royal Society’s Academy to include researchers from across all
disciplines of science, technology, social sciences and the human ities is a landmark
decision.” It recognises that this is not ju st a decision that wa s suddenly dreamed up by
the Royal Society and the academy of the R oyal Society. It was c onsidered over a long
period of time by the Royal Society, and I th ink that was one thin g that we recognised
and valued when we were in the Educati on and Science Committee hearings—that this
was not an ad hoc decision. Again, I will quo te from the Royal Society’s submission:
“There is a growing appreciati on, at both national and intern ational levels, of the need
for greater cross disciplinary  dialogue to address the global problems that now occupy
much of the research agenda.”
That really comes back to what Pete H odgson said in his contribution. In fact, his
contribution chimes very well with what the Royal Society was trying to get at and why
it wanted to make this landmark change. The submission goes on to say: “The enhanced
Fellowship at the centre of the Royal Society mirrors the situation in many of the
world’s leading academies. This strengthening of capacity will enable the Royal Society
to provide a significant contri bution to present and emerging debates …”. I think that
sums up the reason that we ar e here tonight debati ng this bill. I say “debating”, but in
many ways it is a traversing of the issues. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon David Carter
items.text: Let Parekura have a go. We need some entertainment.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: We will wait for the Hon Parekur a Horomia. I did not want to
be unkind; I probably should have sat down. I feel somewhat guilty now for seeking a
second call, to be honest.
To come back on track with regard to the Royal Society of New Zealand
Amendment Bill, there were about 13 submi ssions on the bill, which we heard very
carefully. A number of those submissions we re made in person and were made very
passionately by people who were very concer ned that the object of the Royal Society
was to be eroded. I just want to reflect on the contribution of Bob Brockie—

items.speaker: Hon Parekura Horomia
items.text: Bob who?

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: —Bob Brockie—who is a weekly columnist for the Dominion
Post and is also a scientist in hi s own right. What I would lik e to do is to note what he
stated quite articulately about  his opposition to the inclusion of the humanities into the

items.speaker: Royal Society bill. He said
items.text: “The Royal Societ y might think that it is doing God’s work
by bringing the Sciences and the Arts together. I don’t think this is the role of a
Scientific Society which should stick to its knitting. From my observations there is very
little traffic between the worlds of Science and the Arts and that is all in one direction.
Science inspires a lot of artists but Artists ra rely if ever inspire Science (science fiction
writers are the exception). The Arts and Hu manities can have th eir own Academy but
finance it not from the Science Budget but from  the Creative Arts and Heritage budget.”
Although I think his point is probably slightly  overstated compared with a lot of the
other opposition that we have heard on this bill, it does reflect the feeling, quite strongly
held, that the Royal Society is going backwards in terms of bringing the humanities into
the Royal Society. I think that that view is mistaken. What the Royal Society said in its
submission was right. In fact, the humanities are an extraordinarily important part of
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18843
policy dialogue and other dialogues. As I quoted  before, bringing that in is enormously
important. I will just wrap up on that particular point and hand over to the Hon Parekura
Horomia, and I will give him plenty of time to get to his feet.

items.speaker: ALLAN PEACHEY
items.text: In speaking to clause 4 of the Royal
Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill, I will reflect for a moment on the comments
of the previous speaker, David Shearer. The only bit of merit in his speech was the way
he opened his second call, when he said, in eff ect, that he should not have taken it. It is
time that this nonsense stopped. There is s upport across the Committee for this bill. As
chairman of the Education and Science Comm ittee that conducted the hearings into the
bill, I think it is time that I at least, on beha lf of members on this side of the Chamber,
apologised to the Royal Society for the way in which this legisl ation, which is very,
very important to the society, is being made into a farce by the tactics of the Opposition.
The Opposition is trying to delay debate on—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I fail to see how the
member is addressing clause 4 of the bill in anything he has said so far.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, the member has a few minutes
in which to respond to any debate from the other side. But the member should come to
the point.

items.speaker: ALLAN PEACHEY
items.text: I am indeed trying to respond to  the comments that have been
made by the Opposition on clause 4. The difficulty is, of course, that there is actually
very little to respond to. So on behalf of the Royal Society and members on this side of
the Chamber, I appeal to the Opposition to stop  this nonsense. It is costing the taxpayer
$31,000 an hour—

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: ALLAN PEACHEY
items.text: —$31,000 an hour—while the Opposition unnecessarily
delays the progress of this bill. It is a bill on which there is agreement across the
Committee. It should be passed, the Royal Society has asked for it to be passed, and it is
incumbent on this House to do that in a timely and diligent manner. But all the
Opposition is doing, in prolonging the debate on  clause 4 and in prolonging the debate
generally on this bill, is a voiding confronting the issues of the Education (Freedom of
Association) Amendment Bill.
I think that approach brings no credit to that  party, at all. I say to the member in the
chair, Grant Robertson, who has spoken on clau se 4 endlessly, that he should live up to
his responsibilities as th e sponsor of the bill. He has th at responsibility and that honour
as the member for Wellington Central, and it will not be lost on his constituents that he
is disabusing that responsibility with a smir k on his face because of a greater agenda on
the part of the Labour Party. That brings no credit, at all, to that member. I appeal to that
member to take a moment to reflect on the co mments he made on clause 4, to reflect on
the strategy that is being used, and to question whether he is meeting his responsibilities
to his constituents as the member sponsoring this bill.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: This isn’t the classroom or the schoolhouse; this is the House
of Parliament.

items.speaker: ALLAN PEACHEY
items.text: I heard the junior Opposition whip shouting at me a moment
ago, and I say to that whip that she s hould exercise some responsibility, some
leadership, and some control over her te am. The behaviour of the Opposition in the
debate on clause 4, as in other aspects of th is debate, brings no credit to this Chamber
and even less credit to the Labour Party.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: I have much pride in
rising in this House of democracy and debate. I will certainly put to rest the notions of
the previous speaker, Allan Peachey. I have  just watched someone who has taught the
ABC to pupils over generations in the classroom.
18844 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011
The Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill is a serious bill, as my learned
friend from Wellington Central has pointed out. I wonder when I listen to the debate
between those sciences that were supposed to be exact—only those sciences recognised
through research, and whatever else—and the other parts, suggested as the humanities,
that have been put aside. I was the most uneducated Associate Minister of Education I
think this Parliament has had, because I was evicted from school at 16. But I learnt over
9 years as one of the longest-serving Associ ate Ministers of Education in this House
that snobbery pervades in relation to unrea l differentiations between the humanities and
those supposed exact sciences.
You see, when Captain Cook came here, he used cartography. He would put the line
up, take the angle, and strike it. He used researched science and proof. Yet he did not
know where he was going—he did not know where he was going. Generations before
that, my ancestors used their wills, their hearts, and the stars, and they got there—

items.speaker: Hon Pete Hodgson
items.text: And back again.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: They came back again. I think there has been a fair
bit of snobbery by people like the last speaker , who have tried to be harbingers of the
isolation of those sciences. I think this is  a wonderful and great opportunity for merging
and recognising things.
When I went to school we learnt about Shakespeare. There would be talk about a
pound of flesh, or there would be talk about  Puck coming down at midnight, or some
damn thing. I was always astounded, as a M āori living in a M āori environment, and
wondered why the hell we were  thrust into that long-br eadth learning about somebody
who lived in Italy, wrote stanzas, and whatev er else. We had great stories of our own. I
believe marginalisation, in the sense of edu cational progress, came out of that isolation.
What has survived? What has survived? It alian songs and stanzas  that are 4,000 years
old—the arts!
We can go into the Louvre and look around at  things. Gee, it is bigger than the
Tolaga Bay community hall. We can look at th ings and stand in front of the Mona Lisa.
The eyes follow us, and we think it is great stuff. But it is not science; it is the
humanities. Yet all those mugs go over there and pay money to go and look at it.
In 1867 the Royal Society was started—a l ong time ago. That is why, with respect,
we need to give this debate time. In 1856 the M āori chiefs went to P ūkawa, and they
decided they would mirror those great scient ists. They would get together collectively
and form things not too dissimilar to the King, and everything would be put right. But
what they missed, and what the old profe ssors—Mr Hodgson’s ancestors—kept in their
hip pockets was this great thing about science.
At the end of the day I commend the member  in the chair, Grant Robertson, for his
effort in putting forward this bill, and in getting general agreement for it across the
Committee. It is like the great statement about  the person who is about to inflict on us a
lot of doom and gloom, in about 2 hours and 54 minutes of sitting time—that is, Budget
day. I am not too sure what size they have  used, but there are “nice-to-haves”, like
psychology, English literature, arts, and M āori. Who were the fools in the past who
believed that those subjects do  not have a place in any society, especially the Royal
Society, which was mirrored by our people?

items.speaker: It is like wine tasting
items.text: there is a science of fermentati on, and there is an exactness
about prolonging tasting over a period of time,  so one quits the taste of the wine. But
then people get pissed if they drink too much of it. Or they get a bit wayward. I am
sorry, Mr Chair—they get a b it wayward if they drink to o much. Which is the right
science? The one that is researched and stat es that we should fer ment the grapes, plant
them, try to avoid botrytis, and keep the su gar levels up, or the one that makes us
happy? Which is right?
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18845
I say to Mr Peachey that there is a very, very serious case for merging these great
studies and sciences. We have to capture our young people’s mindsets in relation to how
they should be part of the Royal Society. They should be more than inspired; they
should actually understand.
Imagine a young Māori sitting in Mr Brown’s biology class in Tolaga Bay. There are
two things they like: the Bunsen burner,  because they can burn something, and the
subject of unicellular animals, such as paramecium and amoeba. They are fascinated
because this is unlearned stuff. It is outside the sciences. They are attracted because they
learn that those organisms breed, and that their sexuality is carried out through the
central cells splitting. The cell is surrounded by cilia, which means fine hairs. Then that
person understands that there are two little creatures, unicellular things, flying around in
the air somewhere. That person starts to sit down with their mates and wonder about
how they might trap some.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: Wouldn’t this be more interesting if you said it in Māori?

items.speaker: Hon Simon Power
items.text: In te reo.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Well, that is another point. The M āori language is
not recognised. Shame on you—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Not shame on me.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Shame on the people who kicked it out. It is like
being in Italy, and their language being put under the mat. It is like being in Greece, and
their language being put under the mat. Why are these human ities not important? There
is only one place where the M āori language is really impor tant, and it is here. Why?
Because the M āoris are not going away. Captain C ook’s progeny and all those people
who came from Australia, such as my ancesto rs the Rutherfords, have a lot to answer
for at the end of the day.
What we are doing here, in fine community spirit, is ensuring that these two great
functions are merged, and that neither is greater than the other. It is like the tax take at
the moment. What is it about giving tax favours to the more well-off when the people at
the bottom suffer? It is like not recognising the humanities. If we want to disconnect
from the humanities, let me tell the Scots to get rid of their bagpipes and take those
skirts off, or tell the Irish to stop drinking green  beer. Yes, that is right. It is like telling
the English to stop going to big weddings—all  of those things. Stop doing that sort of
stuff.
This has been a whole lot of nonsense. I am really, really proud of my colleague for
bringing this bill together, for making histor y, and for ensuring that simple people like
me who were evicted from school at 16 will ha ve a chance, or my grandchildren will
have a chance, to learn and to become great scholars, and will not have to worry
whether they are in the humanities or the true sciences.
If we are to say that ever ything has to be stood up and the impact and outcomes of
years of research and information measured, then I say stop feeling good, stop believing
we can do things, and stop dreaming. What is that? Is it the humanities or the sciences?
David Carter is the Minister of Agriculture. We have this great science that says that
if we put so many tonnes of urea on the pa ddock, the grass will grow. We have this
science that says if we pour copper on cattle, they will survive better and get heavier.
But at the same time, the cows piss in the paddock, it leaches into the river and turns our
rivers into dirty, uninhabitable environm ents—and that is thr ough science. Only
people’s feeling that we must  keep things green and clean will correct that issue,
because nobody puts effort into the science needed to correct it. So I am a strong
supporter of the humanities.

items.speaker: Jo Goodhew
items.text: Did the m
ember get the wrong notes?
18846 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: I am not worried, unlike those people who have no
culture, who bastardise everybody else’s dreams  and joys, and who sit on the other side
of the Chamber.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Power
items.text: Steady, steady.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: That member is skiving off. He is not a bad bloke,
though. Simon Power has been a great man. He has run the justice portfolio with an iron
hand. He has used science, he has measured  everything, and he has ensured that the
countables are counted, but he ha s used his heart. He has a heart, this Simon Power. I
am trying to get him in trouble with his leader. He has a good heart, and that is the truth.
That is why Paula Bennett is sitting next to hi m. She is trying to get from him the ways
to feel about the heart.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: It is not easy to follow
a great orator like the Hon Parekura Horomia, but I will give it my very best shot. I have
to say that Mr Horomia showed exactly what this Royal Society of New Zealand
Amendment Bill is all about, which is the bringing together of science and the
humanities, through the poetry with which he  described some of the environmental
challenges that we face through the degradation of our rivers in this country. Of course
there is a lot of science involved in monitoring our rivers, fo r the nitrate levels and the
other things that we might find in them, but  could we have heard them more poetically
described than we did when the Hon Parekura Horomia spoke this evening?
I fully support what other members have b een saying tonight. I support this bill. As
someone who has taken papers in such diverse subjects as biochemistry, the history of
New Zealand politics, inorganic chemistry, and the English language, I have great
interest in this coming together of the hu manities and science. Although there seems to
be—and Mr Peachey pointed this out—a pretty uniform agreement around the Chamber
on this bill, I am not sure that the same can be said of the members of the Royal Society
itself, and of some of the practitioners of  science out there in New Zealand. That was
borne out, I think, in some of  the submissions at the Education and Science Committee.
I wonder whether the member in charge of the bill might be able to address some of
those issues.
When I first looked at this bill I reflected on a number of the meetings I have had
with Royal Society members in Palmerst on North, many of whom are involved with
Massey University. On a number of occasions  I have heard those members lament the
fact that, in their opin ion, not enough young people in New Zealand these days are
engaging with the sciences or feel so conn ected to the sciences through their time at
secondary school that they wish to conti nue with a career of studying science and
technology at univers ity, and maybe go on to undertake some research in science and
technology. In fact, they lament the fact th at too many young people are perhaps taking
off to the humanities and studying subjects  such as English, French, geography, and
subjects like that. I wonder just how much support there is amongst the rank and file
members of the Royal Society for this bill. My concern about that, I think, is borne out
in some of the submissions that the select committee heard.
I have to admit that I come to this debate rather belatedly. This is the first
opportunity I have had to participate in th e debate, but while looking at some of the
submissions I noted that some submitters said the exact definition of “humanities” was
difficult to provide, and that “humanities” was a vague term. I know  we will come to
that matter later in the debate on clause 5, where there is a definition of the humanities,
but it seems rather limited, and I wonder whethe r it is too limited. I think some of the
submitters are right, as the humanities are di fficult to define, and I wonder whether the
member in the chair has some reflections on that. There was even a submission that said
there was no need to change the current Act, because the Royal Society of New Zealand
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18847
Act could be interpreted to include humanities fellows. Obviously there is some concern
out there amongst the science frat ernity that this bill, in some ways, waters down what
they do.
Although the Royal Society proposed th is bill and asked the member Grant
Robertson to bring it to Parliament, I wonder about the process that it used to engage
with its members. I am sure other members who were on the select committee might be
able to discuss that issue. This matter is cen tral to the purpose of the bill. Clause 4(a)
states that the purpose of the bill is to “incorporate humanities into the object and
functions of the Royal Society of New Z ealand:”. David Shearer reflected on the
submission of Dr Bob Brockie, who made comments that science and the humanities
were incompatible.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: It is a great pleasure to rise and speak to the
Royal Society of New Zealand Amendmen t Bill and to acknowledge my colleague
Grant Robertson, who I believe has taken this  matter very seriously in bringing forward
this bill. I acknowledge his work on it and his representation of this organisation, which
is based in the electorate that he so ably represents, Wellington Central.
As others have said, the purpose of this bill—I thought I would remind people—is to
amend the Royal Society of New Zealand Ac t 1997 to “(a) incorporate humanities into
the object and functions of the Royal Societ y of New Zealand: (b) rename the Academy

items.speaker: Council
items.text: (c) amend the standard for the elect ion of Companions of the Society: (d)
amend the election process for Councillors of the Society.” I will talk about one of those
purposes in this call, although later on I will come back to others.
Incorporating the humanities into the object and functions of the society is the core
part of this bill, and I think it is very, very important that it is done. It makes a great deal
of sense. Others have talked about their areas of studies. I di d a degree in social
sciences. Arguably, it would already fall under the authority of the Royal Society of
New Zealand. Social sciences would be seen as science for the purpose of currently
belonging to the Royal Society.
However, when we look at a subject or a se ries of subjects, we can see that a number
of them are made up of different component s. Take the subject of geography, which is
the subject I majored in. Human geography is certainly a social science. Physical
geography is, clearly, a science. And there is something in between all of that when we
look at people’s relationship with the land and how they organise and place themselves
on the land, which is what the study of geogra phy is really about. That can be conveyed
through poems, music, art, and a whole rang e of mechanisms that  one might call the
humanities. So, in fact, many subjects are e ffectively interdisciplinary in nature. It
seems to me that one of the advantages of this change is to recognise that many, many
subjects touch across a whole range of areas, and that make s that traditional division no
longer useful. Take environmental studies; ag ain, we can see it ha s physical, social, and
humanities elements in it.
I want to give a particular example, becau se it is one that I have recently been
looking at. It is the issue of  violence against women. That issue can be studied at a
university, for example, as part of women’s st udies, sociology, or history, which is one
of the humanities. The reality is that it is interdisciplinary. The fact of the matter is that
creating this new object and function of the Royal Society is entirely appropriate.
I want to illustrate that a little bit more. At a confer ence I was at over the weekend
we were talking about the issue of violence  against women. As many in this Chamber
know, it is a very serious, troubling, and pervasive problem. We can look at the problem
from the point of view of the history of it.  What is it that soc iety has experienced over
generations in relation to violence agains t women, and where has it come from? What
has been the underlying reason for the sexual an d other forms of physical violence that
18848 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011
women face? What has created th at? Is it an issue of power, perhaps? Is it because of
the view that men own women and can treat th em in any way that they want? Certainly,
if we look at the relationship between men a nd women in a historical context, we might
come to that conclusion.
At the conference I was at in Australia over the weekend, we were shown a T-shirt. It
was illustrative of what one might loosely call art—one of the humanities that under this
provision is now being incorporated into th e objects of the Royal Society. This T-shirt
had a very ugly drawing of a woman w ho was bound and bleeding, and the words that
went with that were “Relax, it’s just sex”. Th at is a deeply troubling image. I think that
image is quite powerful; the words are powerfu l and the image is powerful. My point is
that up to that point in the conversation at the confer ence we had been talking about
numbers, about the number of women who ha ve violence inflicted upon them. We had
been talking about politics and what the political response was.
While I am talking about that, I note that $86 million of new money has gone into the
issue of violence against women and girl s in Australia—A$86 million of new money—
and there is a 12-year plan to  tackle the issue. Sitting ther e, I could only compare that
with what is going on in New Zealand, where we are cutting funding in the area of
violence against women, where refuges have had their funding cut by $700,000, and
where Te Rito and child advocates have had their funding cut.
I come back to my point, which is that we were having a pol itical discussion on the
issue of violence against women and children. At that point, the T-shirt was shown.

items.speaker: Jo Goodhew
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I am really struggling to work
out how this fits with the purpose of this bill, and I ask for your assistance in that
matter.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am listening to it. It is a wide-
ranging debate, and it has been for the whole of the debate. I am quite happy to let the
member go on, but I caution her to try to keep it pretty close to the bill.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: The point I am trying to make, and I will spell it out for the
member opposite so that it is clear, is that clause 4 states that the purpose of the bill is to
include and incorporate the hum anities in the objects and fu nctions of the society. The
point I was really making was that social scie nces are already included in the definition
of the society and in its coverage. The physic al sciences are already included. What is
being added in is what one might call the humanities. I was trying to point out—just so
the member opposite understands—that many ar eas of study are now interdisciplinary
or multidisciplinary, and elements of all three of those things may come into play.
The example I was giving, and it was foremost in my mind because it was so
powerful, was the issue of domestic violence and the study of domestic violence. A
number of different subject areas, including t hose in the humanities, try to explain what
the problem is about and the c onsequences of it. The T-shirt I referred to was a graphic
representation that somebody had made. They had not done it for shock value. It was on
sale as a serious but very troubling statement of attitu des about violence towards
women. My point was that the politics is proba bly covered, as a soci al science, but the
imagery and the words of that T-shirt, which say a great deal about the issue of violence
against women and girls, perhaps are not. The value of this change to the Royal Society
of New Zealand Act is that it will incorporate the humanities, and those distinctions will
not be relevant any more. Subject areas li ke women’s studies, environmental studies,
and many others that are in terd isciplinary will certainl y not have any strange or
arbitrary distinctions made in particular elements. I think that is very important, because
how we understand things as people, how we learn, and how we convey knowledge is
not in just one manner. We can learn a gr eat deal about partic ular topics by, for
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18849
example, looking at a cartoon. A visual repr esentation of an issue can often convey a
great deal more than a chapter in a book.
So I support this bill, and I acknowledge again the work of my colleague Grant
Robertson in bringing this bill to the House. I think it is important that we debate these
types of distinctions, and I am really l ooking forward to outlining a little further the
definition of “humanities”, which is referred to in clause 4, which outlines the purpose
of the bill. It states it is to “(a) incor porate humanities into the object and functions of
the Royal Society of New Zealand:”. I think there will indeed be a lively debate on the
definition of “humanities”, which is incl uded in clause 5. There has been some
interesting discussion, as I understand it, in the Education and Science Committee about
that definition and whether it is sufficient to outline what we are talking about in the
purpose of this bill. With that, I look forward to resuming this debate later.

items.speaker: JO GOODHEW
items.text: I move, That the question be now put.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I thought this might be a
timely opportunity to respond to one or two of the comments made by colleagues from
both sides of the Chamber.
To begin, I respond to Pete  Hodgson, who in his initia l contribution on the Royal
Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill raised two very important issues. The first
issue was the process that was gone through to  reach the point at which the humanities
could be drawn into the Royal Society to create—as my colleague who has just resumed
her seat, Carol Beaumont, highlighted—the situation where so many issues that we face
today are, in fact, a combination of the scie nces and the humanities, in terms of the way
we deal with them, the way we talk about them, and the way we describe them.
This is not a decision to be taken lightly. The Royal Society is an organisation with a
huge history. I am not allowed to refer to Mr Hodgson’s absence, but the last time we
discussed this bill we had a debate about when the Royal Society commenced. I
discovered that on 10 October 1867 it began its life. It is an orga nisation with a great
deal of history. It is an orga nisation with a serious contribution to make, and it has, up
to this point, been composed of what we would call scientists. It includes the social
sciences already, and that has caused some c onfusion, but it has been, up to this point,
an organisation associated with science in it s most serious forms. The inclusion of the
humanities, therefore, is not something to be taken lightly.
Mr Lees-Galloway also rais ed the fact that people we re concerned about that
inclusion, and we discussed earlier in th e debate the submission of the Wellington
branch of the Royal Society to the Education and Science Committee. It raised the
concerns that Mr Shearer and others have raised regarding the question of whether there
is a dilution of the sciences, and of the abil ity of the society to advance sciences by the
inclusion of the humanities. It raised those concerns as an organisation that, as it pointed
out, had been going longer as a Wellington branch than the Royal Society had, overall.
The Royal Society responded to the se lect committee with a very thorough
explanation of the process. It goes right back to the fact th at the decision to incorporate
the humanities was presented to the council of the Royal Society, it was presented to the
Academy Council, and it was presented to th e fellows over a peri od of time through
2009. At all of those occasions the fellows , the Academy Council members, and the
council members were given the opportunity to give feedback, and at each stage of that
process there was a universal endorsement  of this idea. The reason there was a
universal—

items.speaker: Hon Pete Hodgson
items.text: Fancy scientists agreeing on anything. Fancy that.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Exactly. As Mr Hodgson said, it would be a rare tim e to
find such universal agreement among scientists and social scientists.
18850 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011
The letter from the Royal Society to the fe llows is very interesting, because it makes
the point that for the promo tion of scholarship and excellence in research in New
Zealand, there needs to be a coming together of the arts and the sciences. Although
there was dispute in the submission made to the select committee, the decision to
incorporate the humanities was thoroughly discussed. It was not totally accepted by all
members of the Royal Society, but at the coun cil level, at the academy level, and at the
fellows level it was accepted.
To answer Mr Hodgson’s question: yes, th ere was a degree of argy-bargy, but it was
not at the level that would st op this bill going through, or that woul d make me, as the
member for Wellington Central, on being pres ented with a bill—which I am taking on
behalf of the Royal Society—have any concern about it. I have been  at great pains in
this debate to acknowledge the fact that there was some debate from the Wellington
branch, in particular, about this, but overa ll the benefits to the Royal Society of
incorporating the humanities are great.
The other point Mr Hodgson raised in hi s speech regarded the question of the
importance of bringing these disciplines together. Mr Hodgson mentioned the Royal
Commission on Genetic Modificat ion, which I was also involv ed in, as a non-scientist
looking to interpret relatively complex scien tific concepts in a political way, as the
adviser to the Minister who was responsible  for that royal comm ission. That was the
classic bringing together of the sciences and the arts. In fact, some of the contributions
on the ethical dimensions are, to me, the cutting edge of why humanities and sciences
need to come together.
But with respect to Mr Hodgson, I say that to me the most interesting aspect of this
legislation is the future, not the past. It is  the opportunities that the bringing together of
the arts and the sciences provides for us in the future. We had a lot of talk about
knowledge societies, about knowledge waves, and about how we will add value to our
products. I know if Mr Hodgson ever goes to Westpac Stadium, he will look out and see
all that wood, all those logs, sitting piled up on the waterfront. It grieves him to see that,
because sitting there is the product of nature and the product of science, yet we have not
applied the innovation to it to turn it into something of greater value to New Zealanders.
That is the coming together of the arts and the sciences that I want to see. That is the bit
where the Royal Society can contribute to how we bring together innovation.
All over the world innovation in science has been driven by multidisciplinary teams.
We can go to any country. We can go to Taiwan and see innovation parks that include
not only scientists and engineers but al so designers, historians, linguists, and
marketers—people who will actually bring the concepts together. We do not have to go
to Taiwan; we can just go to see a factory in  New Zealand. I went to a Fonterra factory
recently. The designers and the artists who do the packaging are as important as the
people who are working out whether they can put probiotics into milk. What can they
do? How can they actually make those things work together? That is the bit that I am
focused on, I say to Mr Hodgson: the future of the linkages between the arts and the
sciences.
I turn briefly to Allan Peachey’s contribution.  I will say two things. The first is that I
am not sure whether Mr Peachey was listening to me when I worked my way through
the memorandum of understanding between the Council for the Humanities and the
Royal Society. I will repeat fo r his benefit the clause in point two of the memorandum
of understanding, which states: “Within 5 years the Royal Society will use its best
endeavours to have its Act reflect the inclus ion of the humanities alongside science and
technology.” That was written in February  2010. Here we are, in May 2011, making
excellent progress towards that goal. In the meantime the Royal Society and the Council
for the Humanities have begun working together, bringing fellows together from the
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18851
Council for the Humanities and the Royal Society and working on exactly the things we
have just been discussing. We are providing th e legislative tick-off to that, and we will
do that in time.
I think it is sad for Mr Peachey to say it is somehow wrong for members of this
Committee to want to make a contribution about one of the most important changes to
the way we think about knowledge and future  innovation in New Ze aland. There is an
opportunity on members’ day for individual members to decide they want to stand up
and talk about the importance of science and the arts and humanities together. I think
that is a good thing.
Mr Peachey is concerned about a bill further down the Order Paper about freedom of
association. Mr Peachey knows very well that  there were opportunities to change that
bill in the Education and Science Committee, which might have seen it progress a little
quicker, but those opportunities were not take n. From my point of view as the sponsor
of this bill, I will not take the blame for members of National not taking the opportunity
to progress that bill in a much quicker way.
I will support this bill, becau se I think it is a good bill. I will not stand here and say
that people cannot be allowed to have their say on this bill. Th is bill deserves debate. It
will pass; it will pass well before the time lim it the Royal Society has set for itself. In
the meantime the Royal Society will have the opportunity to develop the linkages that it
is already developing, knowing that the bill will get the legislative passage it needs.
I think we have heard an interesting deba te on clause 4. I know there are colleagues
who have yet to make a contribution on clau se 4, “Purpose”, who want to. It is an
important clause in this bill, because it defines exactly what we are doing and why we
are doing it. I think there needs to be an opportunity for people to be heard on this bill.
Members make a choice on members’ day to come to the Chamber and have their say.
There are very few opportunities for members to talk on their own terms in this
Chamber in the system we have. This is a very important opportunity. I urge members
who want to, to take a call. The Royal Soci ety knows I am taking a responsible attitude
to the passing of this bill. I strongly support it. It will pass in  good time, when all
members have had the chance to have their say.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: I move, That the question be now put.
Motion agreed to.
Clause 4 agreed to.
Clause 5  Interpretation

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Clause 5 is the
interpretation clause. It is where a number of quite significant ch anges are being made.
As members know, Te Ururoa Flavell has an amendment to clause 5(2), which we will
come to in time. I note, before we do, th at his amendment has been consulted on across
the House and there is agreement to it. The Royal Society itself is comfortable with the
change and supports it going through. So I hope that all parties in the Chamber will be
able to find their way to support it. It will  be helpful to have an explanation of the
process and how we arrived at it.
Before we come to that, though, there is clause 5(1), which amends the Act by
“repealing the definitions of ‘Academ y bylaws’ and ‘Academy Council’ ” and
substituting the definitions included there. Th e important point, as was raised earlier,
was the confusion that could occur by having an Academy Council and a separate
council of the Royal Soci ety. The Academy Council is essentially the science
scholarship committee of the Royal Societ y, and the council is  the governance body.
But by having one called the Academy Council and the other called the council, there
18852 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011
was scope for some confusion. Therefore,  the decision was taken to rename the
Academy Council as the Academy Executive Committee.
Some might say that is a mi nor point, but it is important. Those two bodies represent
the different strands of work of the Royal Society. The council has the overall
governance role to ensure that the Royal So ciety is performing the functions outlined in
clause 6, which we will come to forthwith. It  is about fostering the culture of science
and presenting arguments to the Government. There needs to be a body that can govern
that work and provide the overall stewardship and l eadership. That body does not
necessarily have to include just scientists, and it does not. Currently it includes someone
like Phil O’Reilly from Business New Zealand.  He brings an outside perspective. He
would not consider himself to be a scientis t, I think, by any means, but he has a valid
perspective that is worthy of being included on that council. The Academy Executive
Committee, on the other hand, is the harder science end of the operation. It is the part of
the organisation that decides w ho wins fellowships and scholar ships. It is at the hard
edge of deciding what work the Royal Society will undertake within its scientific fields.
That is what clause 5(1) focuses on.
Clause 5(2), as I mentioned, defines “humanities”. This has gone backwards and
forwards a little bit. The original definition that came before the House included English
and other languages, and American studies at the end of it. That is a slight hotchpotch of
subject areas. It was largely defined by subject matter that the Council for the
Humanities tended to note when it described itself. I think the Royal Society made clear
from the very beginning of this process th at it was relaxed about that definition. It
wanted a definition that was inclusive but that highlighted areas that people thought
were important. The Education and Scien ce Committee withdrew “English and other
languages”—perhaps a member of the select committee might want to discuss that; I
was not on the committee myself—“and American studies.” Te Ururoa Flavell has
introduced an amendment that will include te reo, specifically, and also Māori studies.
As I noted when I read out the memorandum of understanding, I think that that falls
in line with what the two organisations, the Council for the Humanities and the Royal
Society, were trying to achieve in bringing themselves together. Right at the start of the
memorandum of understanding, the third point re fers to the importance and value of Te
Whanga Mā ori. It was recognised right off the bat that that was part of the bringing
together of those two organisations. I actua lly think Mr Flavell’s amendment picks up
that spirit; it includes te reo and M āori studies. There could have been an argument to
re-include other things, but the Royal Society is happy with  where it has ended up. As I
have stated before, I am here  on behalf of the Royal Soci ety sponsoring this bill, and it
is comfortable with the amendment that is on the Table in respect of clause 5(2), but it
would be useful to hear from someone on the select committee at some point about why
the change was made to withdraw English and American studies originally. But I do not
think that we should concern ourselves that the amendment is in any way hostile; it is in
fact very supportive of the original agreement of the Council for the Humanities and the
Royal Society to bring this bill to the House.
I think clause 5 is an important one becau se what it does is define two specific
changes that have been made: the change to the structural part of the organisation and
also the change to the definition around the bringing in of humanities. Just to clarify
once and for all, I say that the social scienc es are already there, so m y own subject of
political studies is covered already, and humanities is defined as it is here in the bill and
in the amendment from Mr Flavell.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Chairperson.
Kia ora tā tou e hoa m ā e hui nei i t ēnei p ō. I thank the member in the chair, Grant
Robertson, for giving a lead-in to our k ōrero tonight. I very much thank him for his
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18853
cooperation—and, indeed, that of the Minister —in getting us to the point where we are
at tonight.
I will set the scene as to how this amendment came about—this very good
amendment in my name that I am sure will  be supported by all members of the House.
At the opening address of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues
earlier this week, the United Nations Secr etary-General, Ban Ki-moon, welcomed the
fact that the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples finally had
the consensus it deserved. He challenged nati ons to make the declar ation’s principles a
reality, and to protect and promote the rights  of indigenous peoples simply because it
benefits all of us. This Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill seems an
absolutely appropriate place to apply some of this wisdom.
The bill amends the Royal Society of New Zealand Act 1997 through a number of
measures, including incorporating the humanities into the objects and functions of the
society, as other members have spoken about tonight. When the bill came to the
Education and Science Committee, members examined the provisions and
recommended that it be passed with the ma in substantive amendment to the definition
of “humanities”—basically, clause 5. While doing so, the committee also put forward
some very strong guidance; specifically, to  omit mentions of English and American
studies. Curiously, however—and I take the member’s point a bout it being a little bit
hard on them in terms of that action—in cu tting out and deleting reference to America
and England from this bi ll, one thing that the M āori Party picked up is that the
committee neglected to preserve and protect that which is purely of this land, namely
Aotearoa. That is, basically, where the Māori Party has come in. The committee crossed
out American studies as a part of the humanities, perhaps because we are not in
America, and it crossed out English studies as part of the humanities because we are not
in England. But the M āori Party has suggested that in  remembering who we are it is
logical that we learn about te reo Māori, Māori studies, and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
Over a month ago I released an am endment to the bill to include M āori studies, te
reo, and the recognition, application, and a dvancement of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in the
definition of “humanities”. I will come to  the definition shortly. These amendments
would balance out the bill to identify and distinguish it as home-grown—a truly New
Zealand bill. I proposed, therefore, a defi nition of the humanities which includes
languages—and in particular te reo—history, re ligion, philosophy, law, classics,
linguistics, cultural studies, M āori studies, media studies, art history, film, drama, and
the study of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. That, we thought, was a pretty lo gical move. Part of
that was not to insist on or mandate the com pulsory study of te reo, or even of Te Tiriti
o Waitangi or Mā ori studies, in fact, much as so me may well have favoured that
approach. The amendment that we put up doe s not mean that people must study these
disciplines; we simply propose that they qualify under the definition of “humanities”.
We have developed this amendment not just because one of the submissions received
on the bill—from one George Jone s, I am told—suggested that M āori studies must be
included but because it is pretty unthinkable to consider the application of “humanities”
in our land without consider ation of the people of the land, tangata whenua, or the
official language of the land, te reo M āori, or, one would have hoped, the foundation of
our nationhood: Te Tiriti o Waitangi. This is Aotearoa - New Zealand. The fundamental
source of authority for our country comes from  Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of
Waitangi. In that Treaty the Crown ag reed to arrange governorship over P ākehā living
here without British law. It has also guaranteed the continuance of M āori authority and
sovereignty over our lands, our villages, and everything else that we treasure, including
our language, culture, and customs. In article 3 the Treaty affords M āori similar rights
to those of British people. I quote the Hon Justice Durie: “we must not forget that the
18854 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011
Treaty is not just a bill of rights for Māori. We must remember that if we are the tangata
whenua, the original people, then P ākehā are the tangata tiriti, those who belong to the
land by right of that Treaty …”
The Treaty is a bill of rights for M āori and non-M āori alike. Having at least put the
case, I would like to acknowledge the Minist er Dr Wayne Mapp for his willingness to
consider these amendments. We did not quite achieve the goal, as members will see, in
terms of the amendment on the Table, because one or two major bits have been crossed
out, but it was not through a lack of tryi ng and it was not through at least some
consideration by the Minister. We really appr eciated his response to  the notion that at
least the Treaty section be taken out, as it was indeed captured in, I suppose, the
definitions of law, and maybe even of philosophy, and that that is why we had to
remove that section. There may well have be en other motives, but we will leave those
aside, because we would have liked it to be a part of the bill. But in the end a gain is a
gain, and te reo M āori and Māori studies are significant in terms of their promotion and
acknowledgment in this bill.
As I said, I appreciate the support from th e Minister. I appreciate the work done by
the honourable member Grant Robertson, and, of course, the other parties. I assume that
Labour is coming to the party. I am sure the Greens will be with us as well. In fact, I am
sure all members will support this amendment. It is very much appreciated, and we look
forward to adding its provisions to the definitions in this bill.
Ko tāku noa ake, ko te mihi ki tēnā, ki tēnā o tātou o te Whare. He mea nui tēnei ki te
whakanui i tēnei āhuatanga o te reo M āori, ka mutu, ngā tikanga Māori i tuhia mai ai ki
roto i te pire nei. Ēhara i te mea, he kupu noa iho, k āo, he wairua an ō rā kai reira, he
tikanga anō rā kai reira ki te k ī atu, te reo M āori, ēhara i te mea he kupu pakupaku nei
kāre ōna kiko. Arā nō te  whānui, te whāroa o tēnā whakamārama, tae atu ki ngā tikanga
Māori, he pērā anō te āhua. Nō reira, ka mihi rā ki a tātou katoa i tēnei pō. Tēnā koutou,
kia ora tātou.
[I simply want to acknowledge each of us of  the House. Magnifying this aspect of the
Māori language and, furthermore, Māori customs by writing them  into this bill is a
significant thing. They are not just mere word s. Far from it, a sense of spirituality and
culture is present as well, saying the words are not just mere words of little significance
or usefulness. The explanation of that is extensive and broad. It applies to M āori
customs, as well. So I acknowledge us all th is evening. Greetings to you collectively,
and to us.]

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chairman, and a big namaste to
you. I thought you might have, as is your practice, used our indi genous or cultural
greeting, but I will greet you in mine, Mr Chairman.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Namaste.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: Thank you, and namaste again. I am  pleased to take a call on
clause 5(2) of the Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill, and I am really
pleased that here are the be ginnings of additional free thin king regarding the sciences
and regarding the work of the Royal Society, which now includes a missing link, a huge
knowledge base and the many subj ects that are part of the hu manities discipline. I note
that the interpretation clause doe s not give an exhaustive list of the subjects that are in
the humanities. It simply states that the humanities include certain subjects, and
therefore it does not exclude many other subjects  that are part of the discipline of the
humanities. I urge the Royal Society to look at this more broadly when graduates of
other subject areas want to apply for memb ership of the Royal Society through this
provision. I hope it will be so.
As a social scientist—
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18855
