WEDNESDAY, 18 MAY 2011 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Tax System Changes—Fairness 
1. Hon PHIL GOFF (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: In stating 
that “this Government introduced a balanced package of tax cuts” was he saying that his 
tax changes and the tax system are fair to all New Zealanders? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : The tax changes we introduced in Budget 
2010 were fair. They increased the fairness of  the overall tax system, compared with 
what we inherited from Labour. For example, tw o-thirds of the total cost of the income 
tax cuts went to reducing the tax on the bottom tw o income brackets—that is, on 
income under $48,000 a year. Almost three-quart ers of income earners now have a top 
statutory rate of 17.5 percent or less. A numbe r of groups now pay a fa irer share of tax, 
including property speculators and levera ged foreign companies. We removed the 
incentive for people to shelter income in trusts, and we invested $120 million over 4 
years in the Inland Revenue Department in Budget 2010 to improve the policing of, and 
compliance with, tax rules.  
Hon Phil Goff: How is it fair that a person on the average wage of $48,000, coping 
with a soaring cost of living, got just a tax cut of $28 a w eek to cope with that, but 
somebody on, say, $393,000 a year got $350 a week in tax cuts? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: It is fair in the sense that one  looks at the tax burden of what 
people pay; someone on $393,000 a year pays a lot more tax. Secondly, someone who 
earns a lot more pays a lot more in GST. Th e reality of the New Zealand tax system is 
that New Zealanders on higher incomes pay more in that area, and a lot of the tax 
burden is met by those in the higher-income brackets. 
Hon Phil Goff: Does he think that the tax cut of $13.77 a week gained by a person 
on the minimum wage has fully compensated that person for the soaring cost of living? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: What it has compensated them for is the change in GST. What 
the member opposite is trying to do is conf use a position where there is a difference 
between GST rising from 12.5 percent to 15 pe rcent, and an overall increase in costs 
because of inflation or other issues that might be prevalent—seasonal adjustments, for 
instance. I know that because, for instance, in the last 2 years of the Labour Government 
cheese went up 50 percent—and we had wait ed 9 years for a tax cut. I know that 
because the price of chickens went up 44 per cent. I know that because the price of milk 
went up 23 percent, the price of petrol went up 22 percent— 
Mr SPEAKER: I think the House has heard sufficient on that. 
Hon Phil Goff: Why is it fair that in the Budget tomorrow he is intending to take 
from people who are on low and middle inco mes and are KiwiSavers over $500 a year 
that they were otherwise entit led to, but he is not touching the tax cuts of thousands of 
dollars a week that he gave to the highest income earners?  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The first thing is that the member has only one more sleep 
before he has a chance to see the Budget, so I would not necessarily make assumptions. 
The second thing is— 
Hon Trevor Mallard : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We have worked very 
hard to get straight questions, and starting an answer in that gratuitous way does not 
help. I also put in a second point of order,  which has to do with whether Ministers are 
18772 Questions for Oral Answer 18 May 2011 
still required to address you when they are answering, rather than the backbenches or 
the gallery, and nothing in between.  
Mr SPEAKER : I will deal with the latter part first. It will be no surprise to the 
member that it has often been  a practice of Prime Ministers,  for years, to address the 
back of the House. [Interruption] I am on my feet. I am not too troubled by that, as long 
as members are aware that when I get to my feet they should be silent. The Prime 
Minister did sit down pretty promptly when I got to my feet. To deal with the first point, 
I believe the Prime Minister’s comment was not particularly unkind. It simply pointed 
out that there is one more da y until the Budget. The question asked about a matter to do 
with the Budget, and asserted that something would be happ ening in the Budget. It is 
kind of dangerous prior to the Budget to make assertions about what is in the Budget. 
For the Prime Minister to make some re ference in a light-hearted way—and it was not 
made in a nasty sort of way—that the Budget is  still to come is no t, I think, desperately 
bad. That is why I did not pull up the Prime Mi nister, but I will be listening carefully to 
make sure that when straight questions are asked, the questioner is not attacked. I do not 
think it was particularly unfair, at all, to make a light-hearted reference to the fact that 
there is still a day to go until the Budget.  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: As I was saying, the member has only one more sleep until he 
will be able to see what is in the Budget. The second thing I would say is that it is worth 
noting that if we look at th e top personal tax rate and th e tax cut changes of 2010, we 
see that they amounted to about $400 million to $500 million per year, which is 
something that Labour goes on and on about, out of a $2.5 billion personal tax package. 
In other words, 20 percent of the tax package went to the highest income earners.  
Hon Phil Goff: Are the Inland Revenue—[Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: I want to hear the question.  
Hon Phil Goff : Are the Inland Revenue Department figures quoted this morning 
correct in stating that the tax paid by  17,244 dairy farms in 2009 totalled $26 million, 
representing the average annual tax paid by those farms of $1,506 each; if not, in what 
respect are those figures incorrect?  
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: There is a huge difference between turnover and profit, just as 
there is a big difference between lamb chops and sausages.  
Hon Phil Goff: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER : The senior Government whip should know that when a point of 
order is called, there should be no further interjections.  
Hon Phil Goff : The question was very specific. I did not talk about income or 
turnover. I asked whether three specific sets of figures were correct, and, if not, in what 
respect they were incorrect. I could not have asked a straighter question than that.  
Mr SPEAKER : Forgive—[ Interruption] I have just called the senior Government 
whip to account, so the deputy leader of the Labour Party will also not  interject. If the 
member cannot see what he is walking into in asking a question li ke that, with those 
figures, I cannot assist him.  
Hon Phil Goff: Oh no, Mr Speaker.  
Mr SPEAKER: The member will not interrupt me. I listened very carefully to the 
question, and I just grimaced because I could pick what kind of answer the answer 
would be. I cannot help m
embers if they do not think about the questions they are 
asking.  
Hon Phil Goff : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I ask you to examine the 
question that I asked. It was a straight, factual question about whether three sets— 
Mr SPEAKER: The Leader of the Opposition will resume his seat. I will examine it, 
I promise him, but I am absolutely certain th at what I heard was very clear and I am not 
remotely surprised at the response to it. 
18 May 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 18773 
Hon Trevor Mallard : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I know that some 
members opposite have a special interest in this area. Mr Speaker— 
Mr SPEAKER: The member will resume his seat  immediately. Some members will 
be leaving the House very soon. The point I have been emphasising day after day is that 
members need to think about their questions when they ask them. They should not ask 
the Speaker to help members who walk in to traps when they are asking questions. 
Forgive me, but that is the reality of life. I am warning members that I am not of a mood 
to be trifled with on this. For example, I saw this just yesterday—I cringed when I heard 
a supplementary question asked, because I coul d just see what the answer would be and 
I thought “Surely not!”. I ask members to think about it. 
Hon Phil Goff : I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I seek your leave to ask the 
supplementary question again, word for word, id entical to how I aske d it last time, and 
to let you make a judgment as to whether any of the comments that you have just made 
relate to the question I asked. 
Mr SPEAKER: The question was absolutely in or der. I have no problem with that 
whatsoever, but the nature of what the me mber actually asked, in cluding his question, 
made me cringe as I heard it. Forgive me , but I listen to questions very carefully, 
because I have to protect—I say to member s of the Opposition that I have sat down 
Ministers. I sat down the Prime Minister in  the previous questi on. I have not seen a 
previous Speaker do that. I have helped th e Opposition more than I have seen previous 
Speakers do, but I cannot assist—[Interruption] There will be silence; some members of 
the front bench of the Labour Party will be l eaving this House very shortly if they are 
not careful. I cannot assist if members do not think throug h the questions they ask. I 
listen very carefully. Yester day I stopped the Deputy Prim e Minister on a straight 
question from the shadow Leader of the House because the question was a straight 
question and the Deputy Prime Minister star ted to launch into an unfair comment. I 
cannot assist where questions are asked that  lead to answers on which I simply cannot 
provide any help. 
Hon Phil Goff : Are Inland Revenue Department figures reported this morning 
correct in stating that the tax paid by  17,244 dairy farms in 2009 totalled $26 million, 
representing the average annual tax paid by those farms of $1,506 each; if not, in what 
respect are those figures incorrect? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I cannot confirm whether they are correct, but I can say that 
they are a small slice of what is paid by da iry farmers if one was to accept it at face 
value. The press release put out by DairyNZ said: “We need to set this straight. Our 
figures show that on average approximately $300 million tax is paid per year by dairy 
farms,”. I say to the member that if he does not know the difference between turnover 
and profit, then goodness knows what his Budget will look like one day. 
Hon Trevor Mallard : I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I think it should be 
obvious to you from the tail end of that qu estion that there was no discussion of 
turnover in the Leader of the Opposition’s question. There was no suggestion of 
turnover. It was all about profit and tax paid. I ask you to tell us that you think the Prime 
Minister’s reply was appropriate, and to also  indicate now whether you think that that 
question was wrong— 
Mr SPEAKER : Regarding my comments I made about the question previously, 
having heard all the material that the question related to, forgive me but I do not change 
my position on it whatsoever. 
Hon Phil Goff : Is the Prime Minister saying that the material provided by the 
Minister of Revenue in writ ten ans wers to a member of this House were, therefore, 
wrong? 
18774 Questions for Oral Answer 18 May 2011 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No. I am saying that that refl ects one portion of what may be 
paid by those farmers at one snapshot in time.  
Hon David Parker: Tell us what the other portion is. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, here is the other portion.  There are lots of people that 
work on farms and they actually pay PAYE. There are many other years that go into 
farms. There are many other parts of the industry. [ Interruption] Let me say to Trevor 
Mallard that if he is telling us he is ch anging the company tax rules and the way they 
work for every company in New Zealand, then  I say he should go for it. He should go 
out there and tell New Zealande rs that they now pay tax on turnover, and that they do 
not pay it on profit. I tell members that that will be a staggering speech, considering that 
David Cunliffe was in the paper today saying there will be some remarkable new things 
that we will be surprised about. Wait until  New Zealand companies find out that they 
are paying tax on turnover—what a cracker that is going to be. 
Hon Phil Goff: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Prime Minister’s answer 
related to turnover. I never mentioned turnover anywhere in the question.  
Mr SPEAKER: Enough steam has been let off on th is one, and I accept both sides 
of the House feel quite str ongly about it. I did not stop the Prime Minister on that 
occasion because he was responding to a very loud interjection. The Prime Minister was 
answering in a pretty straightforward way until  there was a series of  interjections, and I 
did not want to kill that exchange. But I thi nk we now have let off a lot of steam on this 
question and we will come to some form of order now. 
Hon Phil Goff: If the figures given by the Minister  of Revenue are not incorrect, as 
the Prime Minister conceded, does the Prime Minister think it is appropriate that the 
average dairy farmer paid half  the level of tax th at is paid by a ma rried couple earning 
only superannuation? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, I just do not accept the pr oposition put up by the Leader 
of the Opposition. As I said, to quote Dair yNZ, which probably has a pretty good idea 
of these things: “on average approximately $300 million tax is paid per year by dairy 
farms,”. The average dairy farmer is paying about $28,000 in tax, I think I saw in the 
release. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does the Prime Minister agree that what stands behind the 
figures on the front page of the Dominion Post today is that a lot of farming in New 
Zealand is done for capital gains, and that is  where a lot of the income comes from, and 
that under our current tax arrangement, there is no taxation of those capital gains? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: It is not true, actually, that there is no taxation of capital gains 
in New Zealand. If someone buys a farm with the intention of selling it, then that will be 
subject to capital gain s tax. It is not subject to capita l gains tax if th ey are undertaking 
the farming business, and that is typical of many industries in New Zealand. 
Stuart Nash: Was the Minister of Revenue correct—[Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: I say to the National Government b ackbench that I want to hear the 
question from Stuart Nash. 
Stuart Nash: Was the Minister of Revenue correct in his answer to written question 
No. 2383 when he stated that the total tax paid by the dairying, other livestock farming, 
viticulture, horticulture, and service to agri culture industries totalled $247 million for 
the 2009 tax year, compared with $486 million worth of tax for the mining industry? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am sure that the Minister of Revenue is right. He provides 
the right answer to all these questions. But I say once m ore to the member that ever 
since Walter Nash was Prime Minister, we  have been taxing people on profits, not 
revenue and turnover. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does the Prime Minister stand by his answer to me, given in 
this House yesterday with regard to the fiscal  impact of the last two Budgets, that “over 
18 May 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 18775 
the 4-year forecast period there will be an in crease in net revenue of $1 billion.”, when 
the Budget papers released by the Minister of Finance in last year’s Budget show that 
the net fiscal impact over 4 years will be a loss of $1 billion in revenue? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I think, actually, the correct answer is that it is a positive $4.8 
billion over that period. I should have correctly said that it was an average gain of $1 
billion a year. 
Budget 2011—Main Objectives 
2. LOUISE UPSTON (National—Taup ō) to the Minister of Finance: What will 
be the main objectives of Budget 2011 tomorrow? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance): The Budget will set out the next steps 
in the Government’s plan to build faster gr owth and more jobs for New Zealanders and 
to turn round forecasts of significant debt on the Government’s books. In particular, the 
Budget will focus on building faster growth and national savings, setting a credible path 
back to surplus, and rebuilding Christchurc h, at the same time as protecting the most 
vulnerable New Zealanders and improving front-line services. 
Louise Upston : How will the Budget build faster growth around higher national 
savings? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Budget will take a number of  steps to ensure that more 
of the growth in future savings is not based on the Government borrowing money for 
incentives and subsidies. The Budget forecas t will also show stronger economic growth 
forecasts, with increases in the number of new jobs and in real wages. It is essential that 
this growth is driven by the private sector. Since the mid-2000s too much of that growth 
has been driven by excessive Government spending and housing speculation. 
Louise Upston : How will the Budget set a credible path back to surplus and 
repaying debt? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Budget will take a number of responsible and balanced 
measures to better target large Government programmes to those most in need and also 
to ensure that public services deliver better  value for taxpayers. In fact, we will take a 
lot of the steps that New Zealand households and businesses have already taken over the 
last 2 or 3 years. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Will he keep his promise to New Zealanders in tomorrow’s 
Budget not to cut KiwiSaver; if so, how does he square that w ith the effective $10-a-
week KiwiSaver tax increase he has already announced? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government has kept its promise to New Zealanders 
and in July, I think, we will pay out hundreds of  millions of dollars of tax credits into 
KiwiSaver accounts. Any changes we make will not affect peop le until after the 
election. They will have the opportunity to e xpress their views on that in an election. I 
am sure they will take into account the ove rall picture: that where the Government 
needs to get on top of a very large overdraft, a very large deficit, it is making balanced 
and responsible decisions to get it under control. 
Hon David Cunliffe : If it was the Minister’s intenti on to seek an electoral mandate 
for those KiwiSaver cuts, why did he not campaign on them in 2008 or perhaps defer 
them to Budget 2012 if he thinks  he will still be the Minister , rather than legislate now 
and pretend he has not broken yet another promise? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I do not quite understand the logic of that. The National 
Government made one very significant cha nge after the 2008 electi on: it cancelled two 
tranches of its tax cuts because of the depth of the global recession. We think it is a 
pretty straight-up deal. We will put the propositions up in detail before an election, 
before it affects people, and they will have the chance to have an opinion on it. 
18776 Questions for Oral Answer 18 May 2011 
Louise Upston: What reports has he seen on  public support for the Budget’s 
direction? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : This morning I saw an onlin e poll asking New Zealanders 
how the Budget had affected their families. I was a bit surprised to see this question, 
because the Budget has not been delivered yet and it might be difficult for those 
families to be able to tell. However, the results were impressive: 88 percent of families 
who responded to this poll were feeling better off as a result of the Budget decisions. I 
thank the Opposition’s finance spokesperson for running this poll on his own website, 
which has now been mysteriously removed because of the outstanding results. 
Louise Upston: I seek leave to table poll results from David Cunliffe’s website, 
which are no longer on line and have been mysteriously taken down. 
Mr SPEAKER: I do not think website material is— 
Hon Simon Power: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The point that the member 
makes is a fair one. If it was still available online your point would make sense, but, as 
the Minister of Finance said, it is no longer available online. 
Hon Trevor Mallard : It is very rare that I agree with the Leader of the House and 
Louise Upston at the same time. I think havi ng the precedent of having websites that 
have been taken down tabled in the House is a very good one. 
Mr SPEAKER: I will leave it to the wisdom of th e House. Leave is sought for that 
document to be tabled. Is there any objection? There is no objection. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
GST Increase—Compensation 
3. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister : 
When he said “In most cases the tax swit ch more than compensated people for the 
increase in GST”, in which cases had people not been fully compensated? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Budget 2010’s tax switc h meant that at all 
levels of income the reduction in people’s in come tax was greater than the effect of 
increasing GST, so ordinary people earning a wage or salary and paying income tax 
were better off as a result of the tax switch. Superannuitants were also better off. Benefit 
payments were increased to compensate fo r the increase in GS T. The only people who 
would not have been fully compensated for the increase in GST were people who were 
sheltering income in trusts or otherwise ea rning income that was not fully taxed at the 
personal tax rates. 
Hon Annette King: If a family, such as the Alexander family featured on Campbell 
Live, received an $11-a-week tax cut but th eir food costs alone increased by $25 a 
week—not just over 1 month but over 6 mont hs—does he believe that  they have been 
“more than compensated”; if so, how? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The family has been compensated for the change in the 
increase in GST by the reduction of their personal tax rates. That is absolutely factually 
correct. What is also correct is that ther e may be increases—or decreases, actually—in 
food prices. As I say to the member, in the last 2 years in which Labour was in office—I 
could have picked any two, frankly, but  I could not get enough data going back—
basically, cheese went up 50 percent, chic ken went up 44 percent, milk went up 23 
percent, petrol went up 22 percent, lamb chops went up by a certain amount, sausages 
and mince went down by a littl e bit more but I am not sure of the exact numbers, 
vegetables went up 21 percent, bread went up 20 percent, electricity went up 13 percent, 
and, from memory, people did not get much of a tax cut. 
Mr SPEAKER: The Hon Annette King. 
Hon Memb
er: Try again, Anne. 
18 May 2011 Questions for Oral Answer 18777 
Hon Annette King : I certainly will, thank you ve ry much. What, then, is his 
response to people like Sharon, who does not think she has been “more than 
compensated”? She is a single parent who is a qualified financia l worker, who knows 
how to budget, who has had to toss up between filling her car up with petrol or buying 
groceries, who is finding it very stressful to  feed her kids, and who said “John Key will 
lose another skilled person. As soon as I finish my degree, I will leave New Zealand.” 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I will be very disappointed if Sharon leaves New Zealand, 
because, by the sound of things, she could ma ke a great contribution to New Zealand. 
What I would say to her is that in the 3 y ears that National has been in Government we 
have done the following things. We have re formed the tax system and made it more 
effective for people to work, save, and get ahea d in their life. We have halved the levels 
of interest rates that are in  place in the New Zealand ec onomy today. We have reduced 
the size of Government as it operates t oday. We have saved billions of dollars of 
wasteful expenditure by the previous G overnment. We have made sure that her 
children— 
Hon Trevor Mallard: BMWs? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes, it is a shame Helen bought those BMWs, but that is the 
way it goes, I suppose. I mean, it was a bit la te once we arrived—but that is the way it 
goes. 
Mr SPEAKER: I think the House has heard sufficient. 
Hon Trevor Mallard : In light of his comment that Helen bought the BMWs, why 
did the Prime Minister not read the papers in his office that confirmed the purchase this 
year? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I am the first to admit that the process was a bit sloppy and we 
should have had better paperwork, but, I tell you what, talking of papers, I was 
interested to read in  John Armstrong’s column today th at Labour is get ting out of the 
gutter. We will see whether that lasts to 2:45 this afternoon. 
Mr SPEAKER: The Hon Annette King. [Interruption] 
Hon Annette King: That is right. Go for it. 
Mr SPEAKER: We are not going to have any of this. I ask the member to resume 
her seat for a moment. Both front benches w ill come to order, and especially, on this 
occasion, the National front bench. 
Hon Annette King : What does he say to another person who responded to his 
comments about the tax cuts—on Campbell Live, for those who do not believe it—and 
who is prepared to speak up? She said that she cannot afford the diet necessary for her 
diabetes and her husband’s heart condition, due to the rising cost of living and the GST

GENERAL DEBATE 
RAHUI KATENE (M āori Party—Te Tai Tonga) : I move, That the House take 
note of miscellaneous business . Twenty years ago a song was released by David Grace 
that has become known as the anthem of T ūhoe. It gives focus to the refrain “Rua 
Kēnana, T ūhoe prophet of the Urewera”. In doing so, it encapsulates the pride of the 
people in the leadership of someone who believed that T ūhoe could and should be self-
determining.  
At the turn of the century, Rua established a thriving community in Maungap ōhatu, 
where land was owned and farmed collectiv ely and all proceeds shared according to 
need. A community bank was established and the people gathered around. In 1916 
Maungapōhatu was invaded by a troop of some 70 police in what the Supreme Court 
later ruled as an illegal assault. Rua was charged with sedition. His trial in the Auckland 
High Court lasted 47 days and was the longest trial in New Zealand’s history until 1977. 
Of the eight charges laid against him, th e jury found him guilty of only one, morally 
resisting arrest, yet he was sentenced to a year’s hard labour and another 19 months’ 
imprisonment. At his sentenci ng, Chief Justice Frederick Chapman told Rua: “The arm 
of the law was long … That is the lesson your people should learn from this trial.”  
A century later, one wonders whether history is repeating itself. On Monday, 15 
October 2007 more than 300 police carried out dawn raids on homes and premises 
throughout Aotearoa. The focus of the raids was in response to what was allegedly 
“concrete terrorist threats”. People had s upposedly attended training camps in the 
Urewera ranges.  
The latest twist in the trial of these defendants is that it now appears unlikely to go 
ahead as scheduled on 30 May. Some are sp eculating that with the Rugby World Cup 
and an election in sight, the timeliness of such a controversial trial has come under 
scrutiny. But the question we in the M āori Party ask is if there is such a focus on one 
law for all, as some parties in this H ouse would have it, how is it that the T ūhoe people 
continue to suffer the long arm of the law with out so much as a murmur in this House?

of stability and certainty in the market place.  
The policy is intended to help the New Zealand Reserve Bank manage a crisis 
affecting a systemically important bank. Th ere are both good and not-so-good things to 
recount about recent financial history in New Zealand. The not-so-good thing is that 
New Zealand was not immune from the global financial crisis, which occurred very 
visibly in September 2008—2 months before the last general election. Lehman Brothers 
collapsed, the Bank of America was in trou ble, the world’s largest insurer started 
breaking up, and the world credit system all but froze. What we are fortunate about, the 
good news if you like, is that of the about 13 triple A rated banks in  the world, five of 
them are Australian and four of them operate in the New Zealand market. So we did not 
have quite the same level of system risk, but let us not be under any illusions. If the 
world credit system had frozen and if  world central banks had not responded 
immediately with a credit infusion, VISA  cards and MasterCards would not have 
worked. Every New Zealander would have be en affected, and they would go to the 
ATM and it would not work, either. There would have been panic here, as there would 
have been around the world. We missed that bullet by a whisker; and it could happen 
any day. It could still happen any day.  
I want to compliment the New Zealand Rese rve Bank. It responded in an absolutely 
exemplary manner. I think that all New Zealanders owe the bank a debt of gratitude. I 
think that the system in New Zealand worked  as it should, and it worked both pre-crisis 
and during the crisis. It worked because we  had what in global financial circles is 
known as plain vanilla banking. It sounds not that exciting but actually it means that 
banks make their money the old-fashione d way by taking deposits and lending, and 
earning interest on that le nding, rather than coming up with fancy derivatives like 
collateralised debt obligations or CDOs, which mixed high-risk mortgage debt, which 
was worthless, with regular debt securities, with the ostensible aim of spreading the risk 
but with the actual effect of magnifying th e risk—in the United States by a factor of 
over 100 times, so that the total bad debt wa s m any times the size of the United States

That is the coming together of the arts and the sciences that I want to see. That is the bit 
where the Royal Society can contribute to how we bring together innovation.  
All over the world innovation in science has been driven by multidisciplinary teams. 
We can go to any country. We can go to Taiwan and see innovation parks that include 
not only scientists and engineers but al so designers, historians, linguists, and 
marketers—people who will actually bring the concepts together. We do not have to go 
to Taiwan; we can just go to see a factory in  New Zealand. I went to a Fonterra factory 
recently. The designers and the artists who do the packaging are as important as the 
people who are working out whether they can put probiotics into milk. What can they 
do? How can they actually make those things work together? That is the bit that I am 
focused on, I say to Mr Hodgson: the future of the linkages between the arts and the 
sciences. 
I turn briefly to Allan Peachey’s contribution.  I will say two things. The first is that I 
am not sure whether Mr Peachey was listening to me when I worked my way through 
the memorandum of understanding between the Council for the Humanities and the 
Royal Society. I will repeat fo r his benefit the clause in point two of the memorandum 
of understanding, which states: “Within 5 years the Royal Society will use its best 
endeavours to have its Act reflect the inclus ion of the humanities alongside science and 
technology.” That was written in February  2010. Here we are, in May 2011, making 
excellent progress towards that goal. In the meantime the Royal Society and the Council 
for the Humanities have begun working together, bringing fellows together from the 
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18851 
Council for the Humanities and the Royal Society and working on exactly the things we 
have just been discussing. We are providing th e legislative tick-off to that, and we will 
do that in time.  
I think it is sad for Mr Peachey to say it is somehow wrong for members of this 
Committee to want to make a contribution about one of the most important changes to 
the way we think about knowledge and future  innovation in New Ze aland. There is an 
opportunity on members’ day for individual members to decide they want to stand up 
and talk about the importance of science and the arts and humanities together. I think 
that is a good thing.  
Mr Peachey is concerned about a bill further down the Order Paper about freedom of 
association. Mr Peachey knows very well that  there were opportunities to change that 
bill in the Education and Science Committee, which might have seen it progress a little 
quicker, but those opportunities were not take n. From my point of view as the sponsor 
of this bill, I will not take the blame for members of National not taking the opportunity 
to progress that bill in a much quicker way.  
I will support this bill, becau se I think it is a good bill. I will not stand here and say 
that people cannot be allowed to have their say on this bill. Th is bill deserves debate. It 
will pass; it will pass well before the time lim it the Royal Society has set for itself. In 
the meantime the Royal Society will have the opportunity to develop the linkages that it 
is already developing, knowing that the bill will get the legislative passage it needs.  
I think we have heard an interesting deba te on clause 4. I know there are colleagues 
who have yet to make a contribution on clau se 4, “Purpose”, who want to. It is an 
important clause in this bill, because it defines exactly what we are doing and why we 
are doing it. I think there needs to be an opportunity for people to be heard on this bill. 
Members make a choice on members’ day to come to the Chamber and have their say. 
There are very few opportunities for members to talk on their own terms in this 
Chamber in the system we have. This is a very important opportunity. I urge members 
who want to, to take a call. The Royal Soci ety knows I am taking a responsible attitude 
to the passing of this bill. I strongly support it. It will pass in  good time, when all 
members have had the chance to have their say.

GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central) : Clause 5 is the 
interpretation clause. It is where a number of quite significant ch anges are being made. 
As members know, Te Ururoa Flavell has an amendment to clause 5(2), which we will 
come to in time. I note, before we do, th at his amendment has been consulted on across 
the House and there is agreement to it. The Royal Society itself is comfortable with the 
change and supports it going through. So I hope that all parties in the Chamber will be 
able to find their way to support it. It will  be helpful to have an explanation of the 
process and how we arrived at it.  
Before we come to that, though, there is clause 5(1), which amends the Act by 
“repealing the definitions of ‘Academ y bylaws’ and ‘Academy Council’ ” and 
substituting the definitions included there. Th e important point, as was raised earlier, 
was the confusion that could occur by having an Academy Council and a separate 
council of the Royal Soci ety. The Academy Council is essentially the science 
scholarship committee of the Royal Societ y, and the council is  the governance body. 
But by having one called the Academy Council and the other called the council, there 
18852 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18 May 2011 
was scope for some confusion. Therefore,  the decision was taken to rename the 
Academy Council as the Academy Executive Committee.  
Some might say that is a mi nor point, but it is important. Those two bodies represent 
the different strands of work of the Royal Society. The council has the overall 
governance role to ensure that the Royal So ciety is performing the functions outlined in 
clause 6, which we will come to forthwith. It  is about fostering the culture of science 
and presenting arguments to the Government. There needs to be a body that can govern 
that work and provide the overall stewardship and l eadership. That body does not 
necessarily have to include just scientists, and it does not. Currently it includes someone 
like Phil O’Reilly from Business New Zealand.  He brings an outside perspective. He 
would not consider himself to be a scientis t, I think, by any means, but he has a valid 
perspective that is worthy of being included on that council. The Academy Executive 
Committee, on the other hand, is the harder science end of the operation. It is the part of 
the organisation that decides w ho wins fellowships and scholar ships. It is at the hard 
edge of deciding what work the Royal Society will undertake within its scientific fields. 
That is what clause 5(1) focuses on.  
Clause 5(2), as I mentioned, defines “humanities”. This has gone backwards and 
forwards a little bit. The original definition that came before the House included English 
and other languages, and American studies at the end of it. That is a slight hotchpotch of 
subject areas. It was largely defined by subject matter that the Council for the 
Humanities tended to note when it described itself. I think the Royal Society made clear 
from the very beginning of this process th at it was relaxed about that definition. It 
wanted a definition that was inclusive but that highlighted areas that people thought 
were important. The Education and Scien ce Committee withdrew “English and other 
languages”—perhaps a member of the select committee might want to discuss that; I 
was not on the committee myself—“and American studies.” Te Ururoa Flavell has 
introduced an amendment that will include te reo, specifically, and also Māori studies.  
As I noted when I read out the memorandum of understanding, I think that that falls 
in line with what the two organisations, the Council for the Humanities and the Royal 
Society, were trying to achieve in bringing themselves together. Right at the start of the 
memorandum of understanding, the third point re fers to the importance and value of Te 
Whanga Mā ori. It was recognised right off the bat that that was part of the bringing 
together of those two organisations. I actua lly think Mr Flavell’s amendment picks up 
that spirit; it includes te reo and M āori studies. There could have been an argument to 
re-include other things, but the Royal Society is happy with  where it has ended up. As I 
have stated before, I am here  on behalf of the Royal Soci ety sponsoring this bill, and it 
is comfortable with the amendment that is on the Table in respect of clause 5(2), but it 
would be useful to hear from someone on the select committee at some point about why 
the change was made to withdraw English and American studies originally. But I do not 
think that we should concern ourselves that the amendment is in any way hostile; it is in 
fact very supportive of the original agreement of the Council for the Humanities and the 
Royal Society to bring this bill to the House.  
I think clause 5 is an important one becau se what it does is define two specific 
changes that have been made: the change to the structural part of the organisation and 
also the change to the definition around the bringing in of humanities. Just to clarify 
once and for all, I say that the social scienc es are already there, so m y own subject of 
political studies is covered already, and humanities is defined as it is here in the bill and 
in the amendment from Mr Flavell. 
TE URUROA FLAVELL (M āori Party—Waiariki): T ēnā koe, Mr Chairperson. 
Kia ora tā tou e hoa m ā e hui nei i t ēnei p ō. I thank the member in the chair, Grant 
Robertson, for giving a lead-in to our k ōrero tonight. I very much thank him for his 
18 May 2011 Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill 18853 
cooperation—and, indeed, that of the Minister —in getting us to the point where we are 
at tonight.  
I will set the scene as to how this amendment came about—this very good 
amendment in my name that I am sure will  be supported by all members of the House. 
At the opening address of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues 
earlier this week, the United Nations Secr etary-General, Ban Ki-moon, welcomed the 
fact that the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples finally had 
the consensus it deserved. He challenged nati ons to make the declar ation’s principles a 
reality, and to protect and promote the rights  of indigenous peoples simply because it 
benefits all of us. This Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill seems an 
absolutely appropriate place to apply some of this wisdom.  
The bill amends the Royal Society of New Zealand Act 1997 through a number of 
measures, including incorporating the humanities into the objects and functions of the 
society, as other members have spoken about tonight. When the bill came to the 
Education and Science Committee, members examined the provisions and 
recommended that it be passed with the ma in substantive amendment to the definition 
of “humanities”—basically, clause 5. While doing so, the committee also put forward 
some very strong guidance; specifically, to  omit mentions of English and American 
studies. Curiously, however—and I take the member’s point a bout it being a little bit 
hard on them in terms of that action—in cu tting out and deleting reference to America 
and England from this bi ll, one thing that the M āori Party picked up is that the 
committee neglected to preserve and protect that which is purely of this land, namely 
Aotearoa. That is, basically, where the Māori Party has come in. The committee crossed 
out American studies as a part of the humanities, perhaps because we are not in 
America, and it crossed out English studies as part of the humanities because we are not 
in England. But the M āori Party has suggested that in  remembering who we are it is 
logical that we learn about te reo Māori, Māori studies, and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.  
Over a month ago I released an am endment to the bill to include M āori studies, te 
reo, and the recognition, application, and a dvancement of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in the 
definition of “humanities”. I will come to  the definition shortly. These amendments 
would balance out the bill to identify and distinguish it as home-grown—a truly New 
Zealand bill. I proposed, therefore, a defi nition of the humanities which includes 
languages—and in particular te reo—history, re ligion, philosophy, law, classics, 
linguistics, cultural studies, M āori studies, media studies, art history, film, drama, and 
the study of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. That, we thought, was a pretty lo gical move. Part of 
that was not to insist on or mandate the com pulsory study of te reo, or even of Te Tiriti 
o Waitangi or Mā ori studies, in fact, much as so me may well have favoured that 
approach. The amendment that we put up doe s not mean that people must study these 
disciplines; we simply propose that they qualify under the definition of “humanities”.  
We have developed this amendment not just because one of the submissions received 
on the bill—from one George Jone s, I am told—suggested that M āori studies must be 
included but because it is pretty unthinkable to consider the application of “humanities” 
in our land without consider ation of the people of the land, tangata whenua, or the 
official language of the land, te reo M āori, or, one would have hoped, the foundation of 
our nationhood: Te Tiriti o Waitangi. This is Aotearoa - New Zealand. The fundamental 
source of authority for our country comes from  Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of 
Waitangi. In that Treaty the Crown ag reed to arrange governorship over P ākehā living 
here without British law. It has also guaranteed the continuance of M āori authority and 
sovereignty over our lands, our villages, and everything else that we treasure, including 
our language, culture, and customs. In article 3 the Treaty affords M āori similar rights 
to those of British people. I quote the Hon Justice Durie: “we must not forget that the

Treaty is not just a bill of rights for Māori. We must remember that if we are the tangata 
whenua, the original people, then P ākehā are the tangata tiriti, those who belong to the

The Treaty is a bill of rights for M āori and non-M āori alike. Having at least put the

gain, and te reo M āori and Māori studies are significant in terms of their promotion and

As I said, I appreciate the support from th e Minister. I appreciate the work done by
